sections.title: Action
items: blocks angiotensin-converting enzyme → less angiotensin II, so vessels do not constrict and the adrenal gland releases less aldosterone, so sodium and water are not retained
the same enzyme also breaks down bradykinin → blocking it lets bradykinin accumulate, and THAT is the cause of the dry cough and the angioedema, not the blood pressure effect
less angiotensin II means the EFFERENT arteriole relaxes → pressure inside the glomerulus falls, which is how it protects a diabetic kidney and also how it can precipitate acute kidney injury

captopril is the SHORT-acting original, dosed two or three times daily, and one of the few that has to be taken on an empty stomach → food cuts its absorption substantially. Moexipril shares that requirement; lisinopril and enalapril do not

concurrent aliskiren in a patient with diabetes
within 36 hr of a neprilysin inhibitor such as sacubitril/valsartan

sections.title: Action
items: blocks the Na⁺/Cl⁻ cotransporter in the DISTAL convoluted tubule → less sodium reabsorbed → water follows sodium out

sections.title: Action
items: blocks L-type calcium channels in VASCULAR smooth muscle → arteries dilate, afterload falls, blood pressure drops

a DIHYDROPYRIDINE, so it is vessel-selective and has little effect on the heart itself → unlike diltiazem and verapamil it does not slow the heart rate, which is why it can be combined with a beta blocker
because it drops pressure without slowing the heart, the baroreceptors respond with REFLEX TACHYCARDIA → and that is the whole problem with the immediate-release form

extended-release formulations give a gradual onset with no reflex surge, but they are not all built the same way → Procardia XL is an OSMOTIC tablet whose empty shell passes intact in the stool, while Adalat CC is a coat-core tablet that does not leave a shell. Either way the tablet must never be crushed

sections.title: Action
items: breaks down in the bloodstream to release nitric oxide → dilates BOTH arteries and veins, so afterload and preload drop together

the hypotensive effect appears within a MINUTE OR TWO and resolves within 1 to 10 minutes after the infusion stops → the pressure is controlled by the pump, which is the point and also the danger. Stop the drip and the pressure comes back up

each molecule contains five CYANIDE ions → the body detoxifies cyanide using thiosulfate, and at high rates or over long infusions that capacity is overwhelmed. At the maximum rate, buffering capacity is exceeded in under an hour
cyanide is cleared as thiocyanate by the kidney → so renal impairment accumulates thiocyanate, and hepatic impairment impairs the detoxification itself

items.rationale: sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil and riociguat are contraindicated, and the resulting hypotension is catastrophic

items.action: Monitor acid-base status and lactate; treat a widening metabolic acidosis as cyanide until proven otherwise
items.rationale: cyanide blocks cellular respiration, so a rising lactate with an unexplained acidosis is the earliest reliable sign, and it precedes the classic findings

items.action: Monitor renal and hepatic function, and anticipate lower rates in impairment
items.rationale: the liver detoxifies the cyanide and the kidney excretes the thiocyanate, so either failure shifts the safe dose down

items.action: Use an infusion pump with CONTINUOUS arterial or at minimum continuous non-invasive blood pressure monitoring, and never run it without it
items.rationale: Part A of the boxed warning. Onset is seconds and offset is a minute or two, so there is no margin between too little and too much

items.action: Protect the bag and tubing from LIGHT. The normal solution is clear and colorless to reddish-brown; discard it only if it has turned BLUE, GREEN or BRIGHT red
items.rationale: Light degrades the drug. The reddish-brown tint is the NORMAL product and is not a reason to discard, which matters because throwing away good drug in a hypertensive emergency costs minutes. The degradation colors are distinctly brighter than the normal faint brown

items.action: Keep the infusion as SHORT and as slow as possible, and question any infusion running beyond 24 to 48 hr
items.rationale: Cyanide load is a function of rate times time. At the maximum rate the body's buffering is exceeded in under an hour

items.action: Never give it as a bolus and never stop it abruptly in a dependent patient; wean it
items.rationale: a bolus causes a precipitous drop, and abrupt discontinuation causes rebound hypertension

items: inhibits HMG-CoA reductase, the enzyme catalyzing an early step in cholesterol synthesis → the liver makes less cholesterol

the liver responds by upregulating LDL receptors on its surface → it pulls LDL out of the bloodstream to meet its own needs. That borrowing is what actually lowers serum LDL, not the blocked synthesis itself

📌 IMPROVE-IT did show a cardiovascular benefit when ezetimibe was added to simvastatin after an acute coronary syndrome (hazard ratio 0.936, about a 2 percent absolute reduction over 7 years), but that trial is NOT in the Zetia label, and the old sentence saying the effect on cardiovascular morbidity has not been determined has been deleted. ⚠ The label names CYCLOSPORINE, which raises ezetimibe exposure more than threefold. Tacrolimus is NOT named, and extending the cyclosporine finding to tacrolimus is a weak inference, so do not state a magnitude for it.

sections.title: Action
items: a relatively selective BETA-1 agonist → it makes the ventricle contract harder, which raises cardiac output and stroke volume
it is an INOTROPE, not a vasopressor → it improves the pump rather than squeezing the vessels, so it is the right drug for a failing heart and the wrong drug for a dilated circulation

mild beta-2 activity dilates vessels, so systemic vascular resistance usually FALLS → but blood pressure usually RISES anyway, because the gain in cardiac output more than offsets the drop in resistance. The label describes a 10 to 20 mmHg rise in systolic pressure and a 5 to 15 bpm rise in heart rate in most patients

occasionally the vasodilation wins and the pressure drops instead, usually in a patient who is still volume-depleted → so the pressure can move either way, and perfusion rather than the BP number is what tells you the drug is working
it does not deplete catecholamine stores the way dopamine partly does, and it raises heart rate less at equivalent inotropic effect

sections.title: Action
items: its effect CHANGES with the dose, which is the whole reason to know this drug
low dose, under about 5 mcg/kg/min → dopamine D1 and D2 receptors, causing renal and mesenteric vasodilation. The old 'renal dose' idea, which has NOT been shown to protect the kidney
medium dose, about 5 to 10 → beta-1 receptors, raising heart rate and contractility, so it behaves as an inotrope
high dose, above about 10 → alpha-1 receptors, causing vasoconstriction and raising blood pressure, so it behaves as a vasopressor
those ranges overlap in real patients → so you titrate to the patient's perfusion rather than assuming a number gives you a receptor

items: pheochromocytoma → the tumor already floods the circulation with catecholamines
uncorrected tachyarrhythmias or ventricular fibrillation

items.action: Monitor continuous ECG, BP and heart rate; titrate to perfusion rather than to a dose number

items.action: Correct hypovolemia BEFORE starting it

items.action: Use a CENTRAL line when possible, and assess a peripheral site at least hourly for blanching, coolness or pain

items.action: For extravasation, STOP the infusion, leave the catheter in place to aspirate, and infiltrate the area with PHENTOLAMINE as ordered
items.rationale: Phentolamine is an alpha blocker, so it reverses the vasoconstriction that is causing the ischemia. The label gives 5 to 10 mg in 10 to 15 mL of saline for adults, and it works best within 12 hr

items.action: Never stop the infusion abruptly; wean it

items.action: Do not mix with sodium bicarbonate or any alkaline solution
items.rationale: catecholamines are inactivated in an alkaline medium

anaphylaxis is the one emergency where all three effects are needed at once, which is why nothing else substitutes for it

items.action: VITALS BEFORE AND AFTER: BP SITTING AND STANDING, AND WEIGHT, BEFORE THE DOSE

items.action: Assess patients receiving digoxin

items.action: Assess for tinnitus and hearing loss
items.rationale: it blocks NKCC2 (the kidney loop's salt pump), and the inner ear runs on NKCC1 (the near-identical version that keeps hair cells in balanced fluid), so a high peak level from a fast IV push injures them

items.action: Assess for skin rash during therapy
items.rationale: furosemide is a sulfonamide derivative, so a rash may be the opening of a sulfa-type hypersensitivity that can progress to Stevens-Johnson syndrome

items.action: Monitor fluid status, daily weight, I&O: location of edema, lung sounds, skin turgor, mucous membranes

items.action: Monitor electrolytes (K⁺, Na⁺, Cl⁻, Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺), glucose, uric acid
items.rationale: cotransporter blockade wastes Na⁺, K⁺, Cl⁻ and paracellular Mg²⁺/Ca²⁺; the hypokalemia blunts insulin release, and urate competes with furosemide for proximal tubular secretion

items.action: Monitor renal and hepatic panel
items.rationale: volume depletion causes prerenal impairment

items.action: Monitor potassium
items.rationale: hypokalemia is the defining risk → arrhythmias, and it potentiates (strengthens) digoxin

items.action: Monitor BUN/Cr
items.rationale: over-diuresis causes prerenal injury

items.action: Give in the morning; change positions slowly; use sunscreen
items.rationale: diuresis peaks within about 2 hours of the dose, and the volume removed drops preload → orthostatic hypotension; the sulfonamide ring adds photosensitivity

items.action: Give IV no faster than 4 mg/min
items.rationale: Ototoxicity tracks the PEAK level, not the total dose, so a slow push is what protects the hearing. The damage can be permanent

items.action: Assess extremities for color, temperature and capillary refill

items.action: Ensure adequate volume resuscitation BEFORE and during the infusion
items.rationale: A vasopressor in a hypovolemic patient raises the blood pressure number while perfusion gets worse. Fluid first is the principle

items.action: Give through a CENTRAL line whenever possible; if peripheral, use the largest proximal vein and assess the site every hour

items.action: NEVER stop the infusion abruptly; wean gradually

items.action: Use a dedicated line and an infusion pump

sections.title: Action
items: blocks fast sodium channels → slows the upstroke of the action potential, so conduction through the atria, ventricles and His-Purkinje system slows
a CLASS IA agent, so it also blocks potassium channels → repolarization is prolonged as well, which widens the QRS and lengthens the QT
that QT effect is not a side issue, it is intrinsic to the mechanism → which is why a class IA drug can both treat an arrhythmia and cause torsades de pointes

sections.title: Action
items: acts on V1 receptors in vascular smooth muscle → vasoconstriction through a pathway that is completely SEPARATE from the adrenergic receptors
that separate pathway is the whole point → in severe acidosis and prolonged shock the adrenergic receptors become desensitized and catecholamines stop working, while vasopressin still does

items: converts plasminogen to plasmin → plasmin digests the fibrin mesh holding a clot together → the existing clot DISSOLVES

sections.title: Good to Know
items: ⚠ CT first, always. Ischemic stroke gets alteplase; hemorrhagic stroke gets it never.
⚠ Alteplase DISSOLVES clot. Heparin and the DOACs only PREVENT new clot. That distinction is the single most confused point in this whole file.

📌 Current intracranial hemorrhage is alteplase's contraindication. A HISTORY of intracranial hemorrhage is streptokinase's. The record had alteplase carrying streptokinase's version, and both drugs are in this file.

📌 Suspected aortic dissection is kept under Do Not Give because every fibrinolytic checklist carries it, but it is practice guidance rather than package insert language on this label. Answer it as a contraindication.

items.action: Assess for GI irritation and bleeding: epigastric pain, black tarry stools, coffee-ground emesis

items.action: Assess for tinnitus
items.rationale: saturated hepatic conjugation lets the salicylate level rise sharply on small dose increases, and the cochlea registers it before any systemic sign

items.action: Assess for bruising and bleeding time
items.rationale: with thromboxane A₂ (the chemical platelets use to clump together) gone the platelet count stays normal but the platelets cannot aggregate, so bruising and a prolonged bleeding time are the only clue

items.action: Monitor BP and edema at baseline and periodically
items.rationale: blocking renal prostaglandins causes Na⁺ and H₂O retention and blunts diuretics and ACE inhibitors; dose-dependent, minimal at 81 mg

items.action: Monitor CBC (H&H, platelets) and renal panel
items.rationale: COX-1 prostaglandins (the protective ones) do two jobs: they shield the stomach lining and they hold open the afferent arteriole (the vessel feeding the kidney filter). Blocking COX-1 removes both, so H&H falls if the stomach bleeds and creatinine climbs if the kidney loses flow

items.action: INR does NOT detect aspirin's effect

items.action: No OTC NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen); use acetaminophen instead

items.action: Never give to children or teens with a viral illness
items.rationale: salicylates impair hepatic mitochondrial beta-oxidation during a viral illness → fatty liver and hyperammonemic encephalopathy, which is Reye's syndrome

items.action: Hold 7-10 days before surgery
items.rationale: acetylation of COX-1 (the enzyme that protects the stomach lining) is irreversible and the anucleate (it has no nucleus, so it cannot make new enzyme) platelet cannot make new enzyme, so function returns only as marrow releases new platelets

sections.title: Action
items: it is a bacterial protein from streptococci → it binds plasminogen and converts it to plasmin, and plasmin digests the fibrin holding a clot together

unlike alteplase it is NOT fibrin-selective → it activates plasminogen everywhere in the circulation, not just at the clot, which is why it causes more systemic bleeding and depletes circulating fibrinogen

because it is a foreign bacterial protein, the body makes ANTIBODIES to it → so it can cause allergic reactions and anaphylaxis, and a second course within months to years may simply be neutralized and not work
those antibodies are also why prior streptococcal infection can blunt a first dose

sections.title: Good to Know
items: 📌 Streptokinase is NO LONGER commercially available in the United States; alteplase and the other fibrin-selective agents replaced it. It remains on the WHO List of Essential Medicines and is still widely used internationally, and it still appears in older question banks, which is why it is here.
⚠ The two things that separate streptokinase from alteplase are both consequences of it being a bacterial protein: it can cause anaphylaxis, and a repeat course may not work because of antibodies.
⚠ It is not fibrin-selective, so it bleeds more systemically and drops fibrinogen further than alteplase does.

items: a long-acting beta-2 agonist → relaxes bronchial smooth muscle for about 12 hr, so it is dosed twice daily at roughly 12 hr intervals

that gap is the mechanism behind the boxed warning: symptom relief without inflammation control delays real treatment, and asthma deaths followed

sections.title: Action
items: binds the sulfonylurea receptor on the pancreatic beta cell → closes a potassium channel, the cell depolarizes, calcium enters, and stored INSULIN is released

it works by squeezing insulin out of the pancreas, so it only works if there are beta cells left → which is why it is useless in type 1 diabetes and loses effect over years in type 2 as beta cells fail
that mechanism is also why it causes HYPOGLYCEMIA and metformin does not → metformin reduces hepatic glucose output and does not force insulin release

the IMMEDIATE-RELEASE tablet goes about 30 min BEFORE a meal, so the insulin surge arrives with the food; the EXTENDED-RELEASE tablet is taken WITH breakfast or the first meal of the day. Confusing the two is a real administration error

(immediate-release) type 1 diabetes, and diabetic ketoacidosis with or without coma → these need insulin
(Glucotrol XL) hypersensitivity to glipizide or to sulfonamide derivatives → note the XL label and the immediate-release label list DIFFERENT contraindications

groups.label: Serious

items.action: Assess for hypoglycemia for a FULL day or more after an episode, especially in older adults and renal impairment
items.rationale: Sulfonylurea hypoglycemia relapses hours after it appears to be fixed. This is why these patients get admitted rather than discharged from the emergency department

items.action: Ask about alcohol
items.rationale: alcohol blocks hepatic glucose production, which is the body's own rescue mechanism, so it deepens and prolongs hypoglycemia

items.action: Assess for a sulfa allergy before the XL form
items.rationale: the extended-release label specifically contraindicates sulfonamide hypersensitivity

items.action: Monitor A1C about every 3 months, and fingerstick glucose as ordered
items.rationale: A1C shows the 3-month average; the fingerstick shows what is happening now. You need both

items.action: IMMEDIATE-RELEASE: GIVE IT ABOUT 30 MIN BEFORE A MEAL. EXTENDED-RELEASE: GIVE IT WITH BREAKFAST. EITHER WAY, HOLD IT IF THE PATIENT IS NPO OR NOT EATING
items.rationale: The drug forces insulin release whether or not food arrives. A sulfonylurea given to a patient who then skips the meal is one of the most common causes of inpatient hypoglycemia, and the IR and XL timings are genuinely different

items.action: Do not crush or chew the extended-release tablet
items.rationale: dose dumping, and the XL shell may appear in the stool

items.action: Teach the symptoms of hypoglycemia and the 15-15 rule: 15 g of fast carbohydrate, recheck in 15 min
items.rationale: and teach the patient to carry glucose, not candy bars, because fat slows absorption

items.action: Teach sun protection
items.rationale: sulfonylureas are photosensitizing

items: 📌 Glipizide carries a special WARNINGS-section statement about cardiovascular mortality risk, not a boxed warning. It descends from the old UGDP study of tolbutamide and applies to the whole sulfonylurea class.
⚠ Sulfonylurea hypoglycemia is long and it comes back. Metformin does not cause hypoglycemia on its own. That difference is the most tested thing about these two drugs.
⚠ Hold it if the patient is NPO. A drug that forces insulin out does not care whether the tray arrived.

flashcard.name: Glipizide
flashcard.indication: Type 2 diabetes mellitus, as an adjunct to diet and exercise; add-on when metformin alone is not enough
flashcard.action: Binds the sulfonylurea receptor on the pancreatic beta cell
nursing_considerations: Contraindicated: type 1 diabetes or DKA, assume one correction fixes sulfonylurea hypoglycemia
Never give it to a patient who is NPO
Assess for hypoglycemia for a FULL day or more after an episode, especially in older adults and renal impairment
Ask about alcohol
Assess for a sulfa allergy before the XL form
Monitor A1C about every 3 months, and fingerstick glucose as ordered
IMMEDIATE-RELEASE: GIVE IT ABOUT 30 MIN BEFORE A MEAL. EXTENDED-RELEASE: GIVE IT WITH BREAKFAST. EITHER WAY, HOLD IT IF THE PATIENT IS NPO OR NOT EATING
Do not crush or chew the extended-release tablet
Teach the symptoms of hypoglycemia and the 15-15 rule: 15 g of fast carbohydrate, recheck in 15 min
Teach sun protection
Antidote: glucose, oral or IV

highlight.headline: Raises blood sugar fast
highlight.critical: TURN THEM ON THEIR SIDE → VOMITING, THEN FEED THEM

quick.one_liner: The counter-hormone to insulin → tells the liver to break down glycogen into glucose. No glycogen, no effect.
watch: Turn the patient ON THEIR SIDE → vomiting is very common and they are not fully awake
Give FOOD as soon as they can swallow → the liver's stores are now empty
Recheck glucose in 15 min; one repeat dose if no response
Know it may FAIL in alcoholic, starved or liver-failure hypoglycemia → those need IV dextrose
Glucose, K⁺, BP and heart rate after the dose
Teach the family to use the kit BEFORE it is needed; check the expiration date
(Beta blocker overdose) Expect much larger doses and an infusion
never: Leave the patient flat on their back
quick.working: consciousness returning within 15 min, glucose above 70, eating and keeping food down

points: Severe hypoglycemia in someone who cannot safely swallow.

sections.title: Action
items: the counter-hormone to insulin → it tells the liver to break down stored GLYCOGEN into glucose and to make new glucose, so blood sugar rises within minutes
it only works if there IS glycogen in the liver → so it fails in starvation, in advanced liver disease and in alcoholic hypoglycemia, where the stores are already gone
it also raises heart rate and contractility by a pathway that does NOT involve the beta receptor → which is exactly why it rescues beta blocker overdose when adrenergic drugs cannot
relaxes smooth muscle throughout the GI tract → the basis of its diagnostic use

sections.title: Do Not Give
items: pheochromocytoma → risk of a substantial rise in blood pressure
insulinoma → risk of rebound hypoglycemia
prior hypersensitivity to glucagon or any excipient
(diagnostic use) glucagonoma

groups.label: Serious

(Misc) ANAPHYLAXIS

items.action: (Beta blocker overdose) Anticipate much larger doses and an infusion
items.rationale: the cardiac indication uses doses far above the hypoglycemia dose, because it is being used as an inotrope (a drug that strengthens the heart's contraction) rather than a sugar-raiser

items.action: Recheck the glucose in about 15 min, and repeat the dose if there is no response
items.rationale: expect a response within 15 min; GVOKE allows one repeat dose

items.action: Monitor glucose, K⁺, BP and heart rate after administration
items.rationale: glucose shifts drive potassium into cells, and the drug itself raises rate and pressure

items.action: Turn the patient ON THEIR SIDE before or immediately after giving it
items.rationale: Vomiting is very common and the patient is not fully awake. This single action prevents the aspiration that is the real danger of the rescue

items.action: Give FOOD as soon as the patient can swallow safely
items.rationale: Glucagon empties the liver's glycogen. Without food the sugar falls again, and the second fall has no reserve behind it

items.action: Know that it may NOT work in alcoholic, starved or liver-failure hypoglycemia
items.rationale: No glycogen means nothing to mobilize. Those patients need IV dextrose, and recognizing that is the clinical judgment

items.action: Teach the family or caregiver to use the kit BEFORE it is needed, and check the expiration date
items.rationale: A rescue drug nobody has practiced with is not a rescue drug. Have them demonstrate it back

sections.title: Good to Know
items: ⚠ Glucagon is for the hypoglycemic patient who CANNOT swallow. If they can swallow, give oral carbohydrate: it is faster, cheaper and does not cause vomiting.
⚠ Side-lying position plus food afterward. Those two nursing actions are most of what a glucagon question is about.

📌 Not every glucagon product is for hypoglycemia. The older lyophilized Glucagon for Injection is labeled as a DIAGNOSTIC aid and its label states it is not indicated for emergency hypoglycemia treatment, because it is not packaged with the syringe and diluent needed for rapid preparation. Check the product in hand.

sections.title: Action
items: a fatty acid chain attached to the insulin lets it bind albumin → it is released slowly from that reservoir, which flattens the curve and stretches the duration

because it has no peak it is not matched to food → so it is NOT held for NPO status without an order, which is the opposite of the rule for rapid-acting insulin
at lower doses the duration is shorter than 24 hr, which is why detemir is more often given twice daily than glargine

sections.title: Good to Know
items: 📌 Insulin detemir has been DISCONTINUED in the United States. Novo Nordisk announced it in November 2023; the FlexPen ended in April 2024 and the vial at the end of December 2024. It is kept here because it still appears in course material and question banks. Glargine, degludec and the glargine biosimilars are what patients are now on.
⚠ Basal insulin is not held for NPO. Rapid-acting insulin is. Confusing those two is the single most common insulin error on an exam and on a floor.
⚠ Clear does not mean rapid. Glargine and detemir are clear and long-acting; NPH is the cloudy one.

📌 This sits in Dosage and Administration on the label rather than in Contraindications, so a question asking for the CONTRAINDICATIONS will not include it. It is still absolute: the label says subcutaneous route only. There is no cautious version of doing it anyway, which is why it stays under Do Not Give here.

📌 This sits in Dosage and Administration on the label rather than in Contraindications, so a question asking for the CONTRAINDICATIONS will not include it. It is still absolute: the label says do not dilute or mix with any other insulin or solution. There is no cautious version of doing it anyway, which is why it stays under Do Not Give here.

items.action: Assess for hyperglycemia → confusion, flushed dry skin, polyuria, thirst, fruity breath, rapid deep breathing

items.action: Monitor fasting blood glucose

items.action: Monitor body weight → changes may require a dose change

items.action: Monitor K⁺

items.action: DO NOT MIX insulin glargine with any other insulin or solution, and never give it IV
items.rationale: the acidic pH is the delivery mechanism; neutralizing it turns a 24-hour insulin into an unpredictable one

items.action: NEVER HOLD FOR NPO STATUS WITHOUT AN ORDER
items.rationale: This insulin covers hepatic glucose output, which continues during fasting. Holding basal insulin in a type 1 patient risks DKA

sections.title: Good to Know
items: ⚠ The three nevers for Lantus: never mix, never IV, never hold for NPO without an order.
⚠ Highest-yield distinction in this whole group: short and rapid cover the food coming IN; intermediate and long cover the glucose the liver puts OUT.

sections.title: Action
items: blocks thyroid peroxidase → the gland cannot attach iodine to tyrosine, so it cannot MAKE new thyroid hormone
it does nothing to hormone already stored in the gland → which is why the patient does not improve for weeks, and why a beta blocker is added for the symptoms in the meantime
PTU also blocks the peripheral conversion of T4 to the more active T3, which methimazole does not → that extra action is why PTU is used in THYROID STORM despite being the second-line drug otherwise

it is preferred in the first trimester NOT because it crosses the placenta less, which it does not (perfused placenta studies found the two cross equally), but because methimazole carries a specific EMBRYOPATHY risk: aplasia cutis, choanal and esophageal atresia, omphalocele

sections.title: Action
items: the thyroid is the only tissue that actively concentrates iodine → so swallowed radioactive iodine is taken up almost exclusively by thyroid cells and spares everything else
once inside, beta radiation destroys the cells from within over weeks to months → it is not a drug that blocks a pathway, it is a treatment that removes the gland
the effect is permanent and usually complete → which is why most patients end up HYPOTHYROID and on lifelong levothyroxine. That is an expected outcome, not a complication
it takes 6 to 12 weeks to work → so a beta blocker and often a thioamide cover the patient in the meantime

sections.title: Do Not Give
items: vomiting and diarrhea → the dose cannot be reliably absorbed or contained
thyroid malignancy shown to have no iodide uptake → there is nothing to deliver the radiation to
concurrent antithyroid therapy → it blocks the uptake the treatment depends on
pregnancy → it crosses the placenta and destroys the fetal thyroid
lactation

items.rationale: Staff protection. This is a radiopharmaceutical, not a tablet

items.rationale: The patient becomes a radiation source, and the duration depends on the dose and local regulations. This teaching is the bulk of the nursing care

items.rationale: stimulating salivary flow flushes the isotope out of the salivary glands and reduces sialadenitis and permanent dry mouth

items.rationale: Framed as failure it frightens people. Framed as the goal it is manageable

highlight.headline: Replaces missing adrenal hormone
highlight.critical: NEVER STOP ABRUPTLY → ADRENAL CRISIS. STRESS-DOSE FOR ILLNESS

quick.one_liner: A prodrug the liver converts to hydrocortisone. It keeps real mineralocorticoid activity, which makes it an adrenal REPLACEMENT steroid, not a pure anti-inflammatory.
watch: NEVER stop abruptly after about 2 weeks → taper. Adrenal crisis is the risk
Teach STRESS DOSING: illness, injury, fever or surgery needs MORE, not the usual dose
Ensure the patient carries medical identification stating steroid dependence
BP, weight, edema and POTASSIUM → it retains salt and wastes K⁺ more than prednisone
Glucose, especially in diabetes
Assess for infection and remember the signs are MASKED
Give with food; watch for black stool or epigastric pain
Calcium, vitamin D and bone density for long-term use
Assess mood and sleep → steroid psychosis and insomnia
never: Give the usual dose during a serious illness
quick.working: adrenal symptoms resolved, BP and sodium normal, no hypokalemia or hyperglycemia, patient knows the stress-dose rule

why_this_one.text: Adrenal replacement, because it keeps real salt-retaining activity alongside the anti-inflammatory effect. That same activity is why prednisone is preferred when you only want inflammation controlled.

items: replacement therapy in adrenocortical insufficiency

sections.title: Action
items: a PRODRUG → the liver converts cortisone to hydrocortisone (cortisol), which is the active hormone. That conversion is why significant liver disease makes it a poor choice

it is one of the naturally occurring glucocorticoids and retains real SALT-RETAINING (mineralocorticoid) activity → which makes it suitable for ADRENAL REPLACEMENT, where you want both hormone effects
that same mineralocorticoid activity means more sodium and water retention and more potassium loss than prednisone or dexamethasone → which is why those are preferred for pure anti-inflammatory use
it suppresses the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis → so after more than a couple of weeks the adrenal gland stops producing on its own and the drug can never be stopped abruptly

sections.title: Do Not Give
items: SYSTEMIC FUNGAL INFECTIONS
hypersensitivity to this product
that is the ENTIRE labeled contraindications section → live vaccines, uncontrolled infection and abrupt withdrawal are all warnings and precautions rather than contraindications

groups.label: Serious
items: (Endo) ADRENAL SUPPRESSION and ADRENAL CRISIS on abrupt withdrawal
(F&E) HYPOKALEMIA
(MS) OSTEOPOROSIS and FRACTURE
(Misc) IMMUNOSUPPRESSION and masked infection
(GI) GI BLEEDING
(Neuro) PSYCHOSIS

groups.label: Common

(F&E) sodium and water retention, hypertension, edema
(MS) muscle wasting, aseptic necrosis
(Misc) impaired wound healing
(GI) peptic ulcer, ↑ appetite
(Neuro) mood changes, insomnia, euphoria
(EENT) cataracts, glaucoma

items.action: Assess for infection and remember the signs are MASKED
items.rationale: Steroids blunt fever and inflammation, so a serious infection can look mild. A low-grade fever on a steroid deserves more concern, not less

items.action: Assess mood and sleep
items.rationale: steroid psychosis and insomnia are common and frightening, and families need to know they are drug effects

items.action: Monitor BP, weight, edema and POTASSIUM at baseline and periodically
items.rationale: cortisone retains salt and water and wastes potassium more than the synthetic steroids do, so hypertension and hypokalemia come faster

items.action: Monitor glucose, particularly in a diabetic patient
items.rationale: steroids drive gluconeogenesis, and insulin requirements can rise sharply

items.action: Monitor glucose, especially in diabetes
items.rationale: the hydrocortisone it converts to drives hepatic gluconeogenesis and peripheral insulin resistance, so glucose rises and a diabetic patient needs more insulin

items.action: NEVER stop it abruptly after more than about 2 weeks of therapy; taper it
items.rationale: The adrenal gland has stopped making cortisol, and withdrawal causes adrenal crisis with hypotension, vomiting and hyponatremia. This is the single most important teaching point for every systemic steroid

items.action: Ensure the patient carries medical identification stating steroid dependence
items.rationale: if they arrive unconscious, nobody will know they need stress-dose steroid, and that information is the difference between a survivable illness and a crisis

items.action: Give it with food, and assess for black stool or epigastric pain
items.rationale: ulcer risk, which multiplies with an NSAID on board

items.action: Teach STRESS DOSING: illness, injury, fever or surgery requires a higher dose, not the usual one
items.rationale: The label notes that patients on corticosteroids subjected to unusual stress need ↑ doses of a rapidly acting corticosteroid before, during and after. A replacement patient who gets the flu and takes their normal dose can go into crisis

items.action: Discuss calcium, vitamin D and bone density monitoring for long-term use
items.rationale: steroid-induced osteoporosis is predictable and preventable

sections.title: Good to Know
items: ⚠ Cortisone and hydrocortisone are the replacement steroids, because they have mineralocorticoid activity. Prednisone and dexamethasone are the anti-inflammatory ones, because they have less of it.

📌 The only labeled contraindications are systemic fungal infection and hypersensitivity. Everything else, including live vaccines, is a warning.

sections.title: Action
items: suppresses the normal immune response and inflammation → inhibits phospholipase A₂, stabilizes lysosomes, ↓ capillary permeability, ↓ WBC migration

SYSTEMIC FUNGAL INFECTIONS

items.action: Assess for infection → steroids suppress immunity and mask fever and inflammation

items.action: (Cerebral edema) Assess LOC, pupils, headache, and vomiting
items.rationale: ↓ capillary permeability reduces vasogenic edema; improving LOC and resolving headache are how you know ICP is falling

items.action: Assess for black or tarry stools, coffee-ground emesis, and epigastric pain
items.rationale: PEPTIC ULCERATION; risk is higher here because dexamethasone is often given at high dose with an NSAID or in a critically ill patient

items.action: Monitor blood glucose
items.rationale: hyperglycemia; dexamethasone is the most potent of the three, so the glucose rise is the most pronounced

items.action: Monitor potassium
items.rationale: glucocorticoid excess raises GFR and distal sodium delivery, which increases collecting duct K⁺ secretion even without meaningful mineralocorticoid activity

items.action: Monitor daily weight, I&O, and BP
items.rationale: hypertension and edema, though less than with prednisone

items.action: Give with food, in the morning
items.rationale: ↓ GI irritation; morning dosing ↓ insomnia and HPA interference

items.action: (EDUCATION) NEVER STOP ABRUPTLY → ALWAYS TAPER
items.rationale: adrenal crisis; dexamethasone's long duration means suppression is deeper for a given dose

items: ⚠ The whole reason dexamethasone is the cerebral edema drug is what it DOESN'T do: no mineralocorticoid activity means no added fluid retention in a patient whose problem is swelling.
⚠ Relative potency: dexamethasone > methylprednisolone > prednisone. The adrenal-suppressing threshold doses in Action (0.75 / 4 / 5 mg) are that potency ladder written out.

⚠ Corticosteroids are NOT contraindicated in infection generally. The label bars systemic fungal infection only, and steroids are routinely given in bacterial meningitis, severe Pneumocystis pneumonia and septic shock. The real bedside version of this is the opposite of a bar: steroids blunt the febrile and inflammatory response, so a normal temperature and a normal white count do not rule out sepsis in a patient taking them. Live vaccines are contraindicated at IMMUNOSUPPRESSIVE doses, which is why physiologic replacement, topical, inhaled and short low-dose courses do not count.

sections.title: Action
items: binds an intracellular protein and inhibits CALCINEURIN → the T lymphocyte cannot transcribe interleukin-2, so the T cell response that drives rejection never gets started
it suppresses T cells fairly specifically rather than wiping out the whole marrow → which is why it does not cause the profound neutropenia that older immunosuppressants did
it is cleared by CYP3A4 → so the level swings wildly with inhibitors and inducers, and grapefruit juice alone can push it into toxicity
the dose-limiting toxicity is the KIDNEY → and the hard part is that cyclosporine nephrotoxicity and transplant rejection both present as a rising creatinine, so the level is what tells them apart

(Neoral, RHEUMATOID ARTHRITIS and PSORIASIS indications only) abnormal renal function, uncontrolled hypertension, or malignancy
(Neoral, PSORIASIS only) concurrent PUVA or UVB phototherapy, methotrexate or other immunosuppressants, coal tar or radiation therapy
note those restrictions apply to the RA and psoriasis indications, NOT to transplant, and they are not on the Sandimmune label at all

items.action: Review every new medication against the CYP3A4 list
items.rationale: erythromycin, azole antifungals and diltiazem raise the level; rifampin, phenytoin and carbamazepine drop it toward rejection

items.action: Monitor the trough level, and NEVER switch between Sandimmune and the modified products without supervision
items.rationale: The boxed warning. Sandimmune and Neoral are NOT bioequivalent and cannot be substituted milligram for milligram: Neoral is absorbed more and better. A pharmacy substitution here causes toxicity or rejection

items.action: Monitor creatinine and BUN frequently, and interpret a rise ALONGSIDE the level
items.rationale: A high level with a rising creatinine suggests toxicity; a therapeutic level with a rising creatinine suggests rejection. The two look identical at the bedside and the treatments are opposite

items.action: Monitor BP at baseline and at every visit, and treat hypertension
items.rationale: it is very common, and a calcium channel blocker is often used, though diltiazem and verapamil also raise the cyclosporine level, so the dose has to be rechecked

items.action: Monitor K⁺ and magnesium
items.rationale: it causes hyperkalemia and hypomagnesemia, so potassium-sparing diuretics and potassium supplements are avoided

items.action: Give oral doses consistently with respect to food and use the same measuring device
items.rationale: absorption varies, and consistency is what makes a trough level interpretable

items.action: Teach strict avoidance of GRAPEFRUIT juice
items.rationale: It inhibits CYP3A4 (a liver and gut clearance enzyme) and can raise the level into the toxic range on an unchanged dose. This is one of the few grapefruit interactions that is genuinely dangerous

items.action: Teach infection precautions and the need to report fever promptly, and remember the signs are blunted
items.rationale: It is an immunosuppressant. Live vaccines are avoided, and a fever is taken seriously

items.action: Teach sun protection and annual skin checks
items.rationale: skin cancer and lymphoma risk rise with duration of immunosuppression

items.action: Teach meticulous oral hygiene and arrange dental follow-up
items.rationale: gingival hyperplasia is common, and good hygiene genuinely reduces it

sections.title: Good to Know
items: ⚠ Sandimmune and Neoral are not interchangeable. That is a boxed warning, and a milligram-for-milligram substitution causes either toxicity or rejection.
⚠ A rising creatinine is either the drug or rejection, and the level is what distinguishes them. This is the question cyclosporine is always asked about.
⚠ Grapefruit juice is genuinely dangerous with this drug, not a theoretical caution.

📌 Uncontrolled hypertension, abnormal renal function and malignancy are contraindications only for the Neoral RHEUMATOID ARTHRITIS and PSORIASIS indications. They are not transplant contraindications, and they are not on the Sandimmune label.

📌 There is no single universal target trough range. It depends on the indication, the regimen, the assay and the time since transplant, so follow the program's protocol rather than a memorized number.

BLACK BOX: only physicians experienced in immunosuppressive therapy and management of transplant patients should prescribe it, and patients should be managed in facilities with adequate laboratory and supportive resources
Review every new medication against the CYP3A4 list
Monitor the trough level, and NEVER switch between Sandimmune and the modified products without supervision
Monitor creatinine and BUN frequently, and interpret a rise ALONGSIDE the level

highlight.headline: Blocks lymphocyte proliferation
highlight.critical: BOXED: TERATOGENIC. EMPTY STOMACH, NEVER CRUSH

quick.one_liner: Blocks inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase → lymphocytes cannot make the guanosine they need to proliferate, while other cells use a salvage pathway.
watch: EMPTY stomach, 1 hr before or 2 hr after food
NEVER crush, chew or cut → the enteric coat is the product
BOXED: Pregnancy test before the first dose and again 8-10 days later
Contraception during therapy and 6 wk after, with a BARRIER added to any hormonal method
CBC weekly for 1 month, twice monthly for months 2-3, then monthly
Hold or reduce for an ANC under 1.3 x 10³/mcL
Separate from antacids, sequestrants and sevelamer → all three lower exposure
⚠ Myfortic 720 mg = CellCept 1,000 mg; they are NOT interchangeable
Fever and joint pain weeks in → acute inflammatory syndrome, so STOP rather than escalate
Black stools or new abdominal pain → GI bleeding, ulceration, perforation
No blood donation for 6 wk after, no semen donation for 90 days
never: Swap it for CellCept at the same number of milligrams
quick.working: no rejection, ANC above 1.3, no GI bleeding, diarrhea tolerable enough to keep taking it

sections.title: Action
items: blocks INOSINE MONOPHOSPHATE DEHYDROGENASE, the rate-limiting enzyme in the de novo synthesis of guanosine nucleotides → lymphocytes cannot proliferate
T and B lymphocytes depend on that de novo pathway, while most other cells can use a salvage pathway → which is what makes the suppression relatively selective for lymphocytes
it is the active mycophenolic acid in an enteric coat that dissolves at intestinal pH, rather than the mofetil PRODRUG, which is why the two products are not interchangeable
it undergoes enterohepatic recirculation → so anything that binds bile acids or disturbs gut flora lowers the exposure

sections.title: Do Not Give
items: hypersensitivity, including anaphylaxis, to mycophenolate sodium, mycophenolic acid, MYCOPHENOLATE MOFETIL, or any excipient
note that pregnancy is NOT in the US contraindications section; it is the boxed warning plus a warning, and the EU labeling is stricter
note that HGPRT deficiency such as Lesch-Nyhan, concurrent azathioprine, and active GI disease are WARNINGS, not labeled contraindications

items.action: Confirm pregnancy testing and contraception before the first dose
items.rationale: the boxed warning is embryo-fetal toxicity with first trimester pregnancy loss and a characteristic malformation pattern; the label asks for a test immediately before starting and a second 8 to 10 days later

items.action: Confirm the product and the dose at every transfer of care
items.rationale: myfortic 720 mg twice daily is the equivalent of CellCept 1,000 mg twice daily, so the two read as the same drug on an MAR while delivering different amounts of a different molecule

items.action: Assess for new fever, arthralgia and muscle pain weeks to months into therapy
items.rationale: acute inflammatory syndrome mimics infection, and escalating antibiotics instead of stopping the drug leaves the patient on the cause

items.action: Monitor the CBC weekly for the first month, twice monthly for months 2 and 3, then monthly through the first year
items.rationale: the label sets that schedule because marrow suppression is dose-related and silent; Bactrim and valganciclovir, which this population routinely receives, are additive with it

items.action: Give it on an EMPTY stomach, 1 hour before or 2 hours after food
items.rationale: food changes the absorption of the enteric-coated tablet, and the label specifies fasting; this collides with tacrolimus, which asks for consistency with food, so the two cannot simply go together at breakfast

items.action: Never crush, chew or cut the tablet
items.rationale: the enteric coat is what delays release until intestinal pH, so crushing it liberates mycophenolic acid in the stomach and defeats the GI tolerability that is the whole reason for this product

items.action: If a tablet must ever be crushed, avoid inhaling the powder and avoid skin or mucous membrane contact
items.rationale: the label specifies this because the drug is teratogenic (causes birth defects), and the same reason puts it on the NIOSH hazardous drug list

items.action: Never give it at the same time as a magnesium or aluminum antacid, a bile acid sequestrant or sevelamer
items.rationale: each of these lowers mycophenolic acid exposure, sequestrants most of all by interrupting the enterohepatic (recycled from liver to gut and back) recirculation the drug depends on; the Myfortic label states the interactions without giving a magnitude, and the risk is loss of efficacy and rejection

items.action: Hold live vaccines and counsel about sun protection
items.rationale: a suppressed immune system cannot safely contain a live vaccine organism, and the boxed warning names skin cancer specifically

items.action: Hold or reduce for an ANC under 1.3 x 10³/mcL
items.rationale: blocking inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase suppresses marrow precursors along with lymphocytes, so the neutrophil count is the dose-limiting measure and the label sets that threshold

items.action: Teach that hormonal contraception needs a BARRIER method added
items.rationale: mycophenolic acid can lower hormonal contraceptive levels, so the hormonal method alone is not sufficient while the teratogenic (causes birth defects) risk is this high

items.action: Report black or tarry stools, coffee-ground emesis or new abdominal pain at once
items.rationale: GI bleeding, ulceration and perforation are labeled warnings, and the immunosuppression blunts the usual inflammatory signs that would announce a perforation

items.action: Teach that no blood donation is permitted during therapy and for 6 weeks after, and no semen donation for 90 days
items.rationale: the teratogenic (causes birth defects) risk extends to anyone who could receive that blood or conceive from that semen, which is why the restriction outlasts the last dose

sections.title: Good to Know
items: ⚠ Myfortic and CellCept are NOT interchangeable. Myfortic 720 mg twice daily corresponds to CellCept 1,000 mg twice daily, and 360 mg of one to 500 mg of the other. The trap is swapping products on the MILLIGRAM number: 500 and 360 look 39 percent apart but deliver nearly the same mycophenolic acid, while matching the numbers would not.
📌 The only conversion in the US label is 720 mg to 1,000 mg. The 180 to 250 and 360 to 500 rows are the derived ratio carried in practice references, not a labeled table.
📌 Pregnancy is NOT in the US CONTRAINDICATIONS section. It is the boxed warning plus Warning 5.1. The EU labeling is stricter, which is the likely source of the common teaching.

📌 PPIs lower mycophenolic acid exposure with CELLCEPT, where the mofetil prodrug needs gastric acid to dissolve. The Myfortic label states that pantoprazole did NOT alter its pharmacokinetics, because this product is already the acid with an enteric coat. Neither label gives a number.
⚠ Acute inflammatory syndrome is in the current label and absent from most study references. Fever and joint pain weeks into therapy that looks like infection may be the drug.

highlight.headline: Prevents transplant rejection
highlight.critical: WHOLE BLOOD TROUGH; NO GRAPEFRUIT, EVER

quick.one_liner: Calcineurin inhibitor → the T cell never gets its interleukin-2 signal, so rejection never starts. Dosed to a whole blood trough.
watch: WHOLE BLOOD trough in an EDTA tube, drawn right before the next dose
⚠ Know the target for THIS organ AND regimen → kidney is 7-20 with azathioprine but 4-11 with mycophenolate
NO grapefruit, Seville orange, pomelo or tangelo → irreversible CYP3A4 block, lasting days
Take it CONSISTENTLY with food, the same way daily; the label does not say empty stomach
New fine TREMOR or headache → the earliest sign the level is too high
Confusion, seizure or visual change → rule out PRES, not sundowning
K⁺ and MAGNESIUM → it causes both hyperkalemia and renal magnesium wasting
Creatinine read WITH the level → rejection needs more drug, toxicity needs less
Glucose → direct beta cell toxicity, additive with prednisone
Check every new drug for CYP3A4; azoles can triple or quadruple the level
⚠ Never swap Prograf for an extended-release tacrolimus product

Add an azole without a level and a dose plan
quick.working: no rejection, trough in range for this organ and regimen, creatinine stable, no tremor or infection

items: binds an intracellular protein and inhibits CALCINEURIN, the phosphatase that activates the transcription factor for interleukin-2 → the T cell never receives its proliferation signal, so the rejection response does not start

items.action: Draw the trough as WHOLE BLOOD in an EDTA tube, immediately before the next dose
items.rationale: the drug binds heavily to red cells, so a serum level does not reflect it; the label states that heparin anticoagulation is NOT recommended for the specimen

items.action: Assess for a NEW fine tremor, headache, confusion or visual change
items.rationale: neurotoxicity tracks the level, so tremor and headache appear before the lab does; new confusion, seizure or visual loss in a transplant patient is a PRES rule-out, not sundowning

items.action: Check every new drug against CYP3A4 before it is given, including azole antifungals and CBD
items.rationale: posaconazole raises the tacrolimus AUC about 4.5-fold and voriconazole about 3-fold; the label instructs giving ONE THIRD of the original dose with either and checking a level within 1 to 3 days

items.action: Monitor potassium, and question any potassium supplement, salt substitute or potassium-sparing diuretic
items.rationale: the drug itself causes hyperkalemia in a third to a half of patients, and trimethoprim in Bactrim blocks the distal tubule sodium channel on top of that, which makes this the most likely acute electrolyte emergency in a transplant regimen

items.action: Monitor magnesium alongside potassium
items.rationale: it causes renal magnesium wasting, and low magnesium both prolongs the QT and makes the potassium impossible to correct until the magnesium is replaced

items.action: Monitor blood glucose and expect insulin requirements to move
items.rationale: it is directly toxic to pancreatic beta cells and reduces insulin secretion, which is additive with the insulin resistance that prednisone causes

items.action: Take it CONSISTENTLY with respect to food, the same way every day
items.rationale: food lowers the rate and extent of absorption, so switching between taking it with breakfast and taking it fasting changes the trough with no dose change; the label asks for consistency, not an empty stomach

items.action: Interpret a rising creatinine WITH the trough level, never alone
items.rationale: in a kidney recipient a rising creatinine is either rejection, which needs MORE immunosuppression, or tacrolimus toxicity, which needs less; the trough read with the clinical picture points the way, and when it does not settle it the answer is a biopsy rather than a dose change

items.action: Never substitute an extended-release tacrolimus product for Prograf
items.rationale: prograf is immediate-release and dosed twice daily while Astagraf XL and Envarsus XR are once daily, so filling a q12h order with an ER product delivers a double dose

items.action: Hold the patient's live vaccines and screen for signs of infection at every contact
items.rationale: the boxed warning is malignancy and serious infection, and immunosuppression blunts fever and the inflammatory signs that normally announce an infection

items.action: Know the target range for THIS patient's organ and regimen before interpreting a level
items.rationale: the target moves with the regimen more than the organ: kidney with azathioprine is 7 to 20 ng/mL, but kidney with mycophenolate plus an IL-2 receptor antagonist is 4 to 11 ng/mL, so one printed number is wrong for both

items.action: Teach that grapefruit, Seville oranges, pomelo and tangelo are completely off the menu
items.rationale: grapefruit furanocoumarins irreversibly inactivate intestinal CYP3A4 (a liver and gut clearance enzyme), so the enterocyte has to regenerate over 1 to 3 days; separating the dose by a few hours does not help, which makes this an avoid rather than a timing rule

sections.title: Good to Know
items: ⚠ A fine new tremor and a new headache are the earliest signs of a supratherapeutic level, and they precede the lab.

⚠ Grapefruit is an absolute avoid, not a spacing problem. One glass is enough, the effect lasts days, and it extends to Seville oranges, pomelo and tangelo, which is how it gets missed in marmalade and citrus juice blends.

📌 Prograf's boxed warning is malignancies and serious infections. ASTAGRAF XL, the extended-release product, carries a longer boxed warning that adds ↑ mortality in female LIVER transplant patients and is not approved in liver transplant. Do not let that one migrate onto Prograf.
📌 The US label does NOT state when to draw the trough. The 12 hour rule every reference prints is practice standard and non-US labeling. It is correct; it is just not from the US label.
📌 Hypomagnesemia runs 34 to 48 percent and is left out of most nursing references. It is the link between this drug, a loop diuretic, and a long QT.
⚠ Steroids INDUCE CYP3A4, so a prednisone taper lowers that induction and the tacrolimus level RISES with no dose change. A level that climbs mid-taper may be de-induction rather than a dosing error.

items.action: Assess pain (PQRSTU) and temperature before and after administration

items.action: RESPIRATORY RATE BEFORE AND AFTER: RESPIRATORY RATE AND SEDATION LEVEL BEFORE EVERY DOSE, AND AGAIN AFTER
items.rationale: Hold and notify for RR <12; naloxone for RR <8 with unresponsiveness → (Resp) sedation precedes respiratory depression. A sedation scale catches it earlier than a respiratory rate does

items.action: Confirm OPIOID TOLERANCE before any patch is applied
items.rationale: Opioid-tolerant means at least 60 mg of oral morphine daily, or the equivalent, for a week or longer. A patch on an opioid-naive patient has killed people, and it is the most heavily tested fact about this drug

items.action: Check for BENZODIAZEPINES and other CNS depressants
items.rationale: A boxed warning on both drug classes. The combination produces profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma and death

items.action: Assess BP and pulse before the dose, and again after
items.rationale: Opioids release histamine and reduce vascular tone, so the pressure falls, and it falls furthest in a patient who is already volume depleted or upright. Taken with the sedation, that is how an ordinary dose becomes a fall

items.action: Never use a patch for acute, post-operative or intermittent pain
items.rationale: Labeled contraindications. The patch takes 12 to 24 hr to work and 17 hr to wash out, which is the opposite of what acute pain needs

items.action: Keep the patch and the surrounding skin away from HEAT: no heating pads, electric blankets, hot baths, saunas or prolonged sun, and assess any patient who develops a FEVER
items.rationale: Heat ↑ absorption and has caused fatal overdose. This is a boxed warning, and a febrile patient wearing a patch needs closer monitoring and possibly a dose reduction

items.action: Apply the patch to clean, dry, intact, non-irritated, non-irradiated skin; rotate sites; date it; and remove the OLD patch
items.rationale: A forgotten patch stacked under a new one doubles the dose. Count them on and count them off

items.action: Dispose of used patches by folding the adhesive together and flushing or using a take-back program
items.rationale: A used patch still contains drug. Accidental exposure, especially in a child, can be fatal, and that is a boxed warning

items.action: Start a bowel regimen with the first dose
items.rationale: constipation is the one opioid effect tolerance never develops to

items.action: (IV) Give it slowly and watch for chest wall rigidity
items.rationale: rapid administration of a potent synthetic opioid causes rigidity that defeats bag-mask ventilation

items.action: Do not ↑ the patch dose sooner than 3 days after the first application
items.rationale: it takes up to 6 days for levels to equilibrate on a new dose, so early escalation stacks onto a rising level

sections.title: Action
items: full mu opioid agonist → ordinary opioid analgesia, with less effect on the biliary and ureteral sphincters than morphine, which is the historical reason it was used in pancreatitis and renal colic

it is metabolized to NORMEPERIDINE, which has about HALF the analgesic potency of meperidine but roughly TWICE its convulsant potency, and a half-life of 15 to 20 hr → so with repeated dosing you accumulate far more seizure risk than pain relief, and the result is tremor, myoclonus, agitation and SEIZURES
normeperidine is cleared by the KIDNEY → so renal impairment and older age make accumulation much faster, and the seizures can happen at ordinary doses
this is the only common opioid whose metabolite causes seizures, which is why meperidine has largely been abandoned for anything but short, specific uses

concurrent MONOAMINE OXIDASE INHIBITORS, or use of an MAOI within the last 14 days → this combination has caused coma, severe respiratory depression, cyanosis and hypotension
known or suspected GI obstruction including paralytic ileus
hypersensitivity to meperidine

items: ⚠ Answer RR <12 on a fundamentals exam, but know why it is the weaker sign: in an opioid-naive patient the rate can stay normal through real hypoventilation, so RISING SEDATION is the earlier warning. Assess sedation before you wake the patient to count breaths.

⚠ Meperidine's problem is its metabolite. Normeperidine gives about half the analgesia and twice the seizure risk, is renally cleared, and has a half-life of 15 to 20 hr. The accumulating ratio of risk to benefit is why this drug has mostly been retired.
⚠ MAOI plus meperidine is a classic lethal combination and a labeled contraindication.
📌 The widely taught '48-hour limit' and '600 mg per 24 hours' ceiling are NOT in FDA labeling. They are institutional and guideline conventions, and good ones, but do not cite them as label facts.

items.action: The half-life far outlasts the analgesic effect, so it accumulates

sections.title: Action
items: inhibits prostaglandin synthesis by blocking both COX-1 and COX-2 → ↓ pain, fever, and inflammation
COX-2 blockade is the therapeutic part → less inflammatory prostaglandin at the site of injury

COX-1 blockade is where every adverse effect comes from: COX-1 prostaglandins protect gastric mucosa (→ ulceration and bleeding), maintain renal blood flow (→ acute kidney injury, especially in dehydration, HF, or with an ACE inhibitor and diuretic), and make platelet thromboxane (→ bleeding)
longer half-life than ibuprofen → twice-daily dosing, which makes it the arthritis choice, but it also means longer GI and renal exposure per day

items.action: Assess pain and temperature before and after administration
items.rationale: COX blockade (the prostaglandin-making enzymes) cuts prostaglandin at the injury site and resets the hypothalamic thermostat, so pain score and temperature are the measurable endpoints

items.action: Assess for rhinitis, asthma, and urticaria in patients with asthma
items.rationale: samter's triad (asthma + aspirin sensitivity + nasal polyps) means high risk of reacting to any NSAID

items.action: Assess for S/S of HF
items.rationale: the sodium and water retained from prostaglandin blockade raise preload, which a failing ventricle cannot move → dyspnea, crackles, weight gain, JVD

items.action: Assess for S/S of GI bleeding (tarry stools, dizziness, hypotension)
items.rationale: COX-1 (the enzyme that protects the stomach lining) blockade strips the prostaglandins maintaining gastric mucus and bicarbonate, inhibited thromboxane (the platelet clumping chemical) lets the erosion bleed, and the drug's own analgesia masks the dyspepsia that would have warned you

items.action: Assess for hypersensitivity, rash (DRESS, SJS, TEN, GBFDE), anaphylaxis
items.rationale: COX blockade shunts arachidonic acid to leukotrienes → pseudoallergic urticaria and bronchospasm; DRESS, SJS, and TEN are separate dose-independent T-cell reactions

items.action: Monitor BP and edema at baseline and periodically
items.rationale: renal prostaglandin loss cuts sodium excretion and renal blood flow → water retention and rising BP, which also blunts diuretics and ACE inhibitors

items.action: Monitor renal and hepatic panel and K⁺
items.rationale: ↓ renal blood flow → impairment and hyperkalemia

items.action: Administer lowest effective dose for the shortest duration; give with food
items.rationale: mucosal injury is systemic from COX-1 (the enzyme that protects the stomach lining) blockade, so food buffers only direct contact and does not prevent ulceration; GI and renal risk both scale with dose and duration, which is what limits them

sections.title: Action
items: binds mu opiate receptors in the CNS → alters perception of and response to painful stimuli, plus generalized CNS depression

hypersensitivity to oxycodone, such as anaphylaxis
significant respiratory depression → opioids suppress respiratory drive
hypercarbia → the patient is already failing to clear CO₂, and an opioid blunts the drive that is barely keeping up

sections.title: Action
items: blocks voltage-gated sodium channels in their inactivated state → neurons that are firing repetitively cannot keep firing, while normal neurons are left alone
that same stabilizing effect on sensory nerves is why it is FIRST-LINE for trigeminal neuralgia → it quiets the misfiring nerve rather than masking the pain

it INDUCES its own metabolism → the level falls over the first weeks on a fixed dose, so the dose has to be raised. This is called autoinduction, and while phenobarbital and primidone do it to a lesser degree, carbamazepine is the one where it genuinely changes management
it is also a broad CYP450 inducer → it lowers the level of oral contraceptives, warfarin, many other anticonvulsants and much else, so the interaction list is long

sections.title: Do Not Give

items.action: Assess for fever, lymphadenopathy, facial swelling or organ involvement alongside a rash
items.rationale: multiorgan hypersensitivity and DRESS can present without a dramatic rash, and they are fatal if the drug continues

items.action: Assess mood and suicidality, particularly early and in anyone 24 or younger
items.rationale: lamotrigine carries the FDA antiepileptic class suicidality warning, which the pooled data put at roughly twice the placebo rate with no age threshold; its BOXED warning is serious rash, which is why any new rash stops the drug

items.action: Check the hormonal contraception history
items.rationale: estrogen-containing contraceptives lower the lamotrigine level, and starting or stopping one changes the dose requirement

items.action: Follow the titration schedule EXACTLY and never accelerate it
items.rationale: The boxed warning names the two modifiable risk factors: exceeding the starting dose and exceeding the escalation rate. A typical adult schedule is 25 mg daily for 2 weeks, 50 mg daily for 2 weeks, then ↑ of 50 mg every 1 to 2 weeks. The slowness IS the safety

items.action: HALVE the dose and slow the titration if the patient is also on valproate
items.rationale: Valproate inhibits lamotrigine's clearance and roughly doubles its level. It is the single strongest risk factor for the serious rash

items.action: RESTART the full titration from the beginning if the patient has missed doses for more than 5 half-lives
items.rationale: Tolerance to the rash is lost when the drug stops. Resuming at the old dose after a gap is a recognized cause of SJS, and patients do exactly that

items.action: Do NOT expect to follow a blood level
items.rationale: The label states that a therapeutic plasma concentration range has not been established. Any range quoted for lamotrigine is not from the label, and the dose is adjusted by response

items.action: Teach the patient to report ANY rash immediately and to stop the drug
items.rationale: The label says to discontinue at the first sign of rash unless it is clearly not drug related. Most serious rashes appear in weeks 2 to 8, so that window needs explicit attention

items.action: Teach that stopping abruptly can precipitate seizures
items.rationale: taper over at least 2 weeks unless safety requires faster

sections.title: I Know It's Working Because
items: seizure frequency reduced

items.label: Black box
items.value: serious skin rashes → rashes requiring hospitalization and discontinuation have occurred, including Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Incidence is about 0.3 to 0.8 percent in children 2 to 17 and 0.08 to 0.3 percent in adults. Nearly all life-threatening rashes occur within 2 to 8 weeks of initiation. Discontinue at the first sign of rash unless it is clearly not drug related. The risk is ↑ by concurrent valproate, by exceeding the recommended initial dose, and by exceeding the recommended rate of dose escalation

sections.title: Good to Know
items: ⚠ The titration schedule is the safety feature. Going faster to help the patient sooner is the single most dangerous thing you can do with this drug.
⚠ A gap in doses means starting the titration over. Patients who stop for two weeks and restart at their old dose are the classic SJS case.
⚠ Valproate doubles the level. Lamotrigine plus valproate means half the dose and a slower climb.
📌 There is NO established therapeutic range for lamotrigine, unlike carbamazepine, phenytoin and valproate. The label says so explicitly.

items.action: Monitor notable changes in behavior indicating emergence or worsening of suicidal thoughts, behavior, or depression

items.action: Monitor CBC, hepatic panel, and albumin

items.action: (IV) INFUSE NO FASTER THAN 50 MG/MIN IN AN ADULT, AND SLOWER THAN THAT IN AN OLDER, CRITICALLY ILL OR HYPOTENSIVE PATIENT. NEVER IN D5W

items.action: (IV) Use a large-bore patent line and assess the site constantly → stop for any pain, burning, or discoloration
items.rationale: Purple glove syndrome: progressive discoloration and edema distal to the site that can progress to limb ischemia. Highly alkaline drug

items.action: Hold enteral feedings 1-2 hr before and after a PO dose
items.rationale: tube feeds bind phenytoin and can drop the level into the subtherapeutic range → breakthrough seizures

items.action: (Education) Meticulous oral hygiene and regular dental visits

items.action: (Education) Never stop abruptly → always taper

items.action: ASSESS FOR ACUTE ANGLE-CLOSURE GLAUCOMA → SUDDEN EYE PAIN, BLURRED VISION, ↓ VISUAL ACUITY, ESPECIALLY IN THE FIRST MONTH
items.rationale: This is an ophthalmic EMERGENCY and can cause permanent vision loss. It happens early; a patient reporting new eye pain on topiramate needs to be seen immediately

items.action: Assess for ↓ sweating and monitor temperature, especially in children and hot environments
items.rationale: Oligohidrosis → (Metabolic) hyperthermia. Carbonic anhydrase inhibition impairs sweating, and sweating is the body's main cooling route

items.action: Assess for cognitive slowing and word-finding difficulty
items.rationale: it enhances GABA (the brain's braking signal) and blocks AMPA and kainate glutamate receptors (the accelerating ones), which slows cortical processing, so word-finding and memory trouble track the dose and worsen with fast titration

items.action: Assess for suicidality
items.rationale: anticonvulsants carry an FDA warning for emergent suicidal ideation, and this drug's own cognitive and mood blunting can compound it

items.action: Monitor for notable behavior changes indicating emergence or worsening of suicidal thoughts, behavior, or depression
items.rationale: SUICIDAL THOUGHTS/BEHAVIORS; a class effect of anticonvulsants

items.action: Monitor serum bicarbonate for metabolic acidosis
items.rationale: carbonic anhydrase inhibition causes a non-anion-gap metabolic acidosis; symptoms are fatigue, anorexia, and hyperventilation

items.action: Monitor hepatic panel and CBC
items.rationale: topiramate is partly hepatically metabolized and is linked in postmarketing reports to thrombocytopenia and bleeding, so platelets and transaminases (AST and ALT) are both followed; mechanism unestablished

items.action: Monitor weight
items.rationale: weight loss is predictable and dose-related

items.action: (Education) Push fluids
items.rationale: Nephrolithiasis. Carbonic anhydrase inhibition alkalinizes urine and ↓ citrate → calcium phosphate stones form. Dilute urine is the defense

items.action: (Education) Never stop abruptly → risk of status epilepticus; always taper
items.rationale: withdrawal removes sodium channel blockade, GABA (the brain's main braking signal) enhancement, and AMPA/kainate blockade all at once, leaving the cortex abruptly hyperexcitable

items.action: (Bipolar disorder) Assess mental status and cognitive abilities

items.action: Assess suicidal tendencies, ↑ risk in Pts. ≤24 yr

items.action: Verify pregnancy status and effective contraception in anyone of reproductive potential

items.action: (Migraine prophylaxis) Monitor frequency and intensity of migraine headaches

items.action: Monitor for S/S of hepatotoxicity → malaise, weakness, lethargy, facial edema, anorexia, vomiting; check hepatic panel at baseline and frequently in the first 6 mo

items.action: Monitor for S/S of pancreatitis → abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, anorexia; check amylase and lipase if suspected
items.rationale: PANCREATITIS and the second black box. It can be hemorrhagic, rapid, and fatal, and can occur at any point in therapy

items.action: Monitor serum ammonia if the patient becomes lethargic, confused, or vomits unexplainedly
items.rationale: HYPERAMMONEMIA can occur with a normal hepatic panel and a therapeutic valproate level; it presents as encephalopathy

items.action: Monitor CBC with platelets and assess for bruising and bleeding
items.rationale: thrombocytopenia is dose-related; check before surgery

items.action: Monitor for skin rash → DRESS; discontinue immediately
items.rationale: DRESS, SJS and TEN from valproate are delayed T-cell-mediated hypersensitivity reactions, not dose-related, so a new rash means stopping before epidermal detachment begins

items.action: Monitor serum valproate levels (50-100 mcg/mL)
items.rationale: one of only two drugs in this section with a level to follow; confirms adherence and guides dosing

items.action: (Education) Never stop abruptly → always taper
items.rationale: abruptly losing raised GABA (the brain's main braking signal) plus Na⁺ and T-type calcium blockade leaves thalamocortical and cortical circuits unopposed → withdrawal seizures

sections.title: Good to Know
items: ⚠ The RR <12 figure students are taught for benzodiazepines is borrowed from opioid teaching; no label or drug guide states it. What is real is that the danger multiplies when a benzodiazepine and an opioid are given together.

sections.title: Good to Know
items: ⚠ CITALOPRAM is the SSRI with a QT-driven dose restriction: FDA capped it at 40 mg, and at 20 mg over age 60, in hepatic impairment, or in CYP2C19 poor metabolizers. Escitalopram has a dose ceiling too, but for a different reason. If a question pairs an SSRI with an ECG and a dose limit, it is citalopram.
⚠ Escitalopram is the S-enantiomer of citalopram, the same drug family at roughly half the dose. Same family, different QT story, which is exactly the kind of near-pair an exam likes.

📌 US and UK regulators disagree about escitalopram and QT. The FDA label carries no QT warning subsection and does not tie the dose ceiling to QT. The UK MHRA does: it caps escitalopram at 10 mg daily over age 65 and in hepatic impairment, and CONTRAINDICATES combining it with QT-prolonging medicines. For a US exam, answer with the FDA position and remember that citalopram is the QT drug. For clinical reasoning, treat an escitalopram patient who is also on a QT-prolonging drug as a real concern, because that is the one point both regulators agree on.

📌 The QT restrictions people attach to escitalopram are citalopram's. Citalopram carries the dose ceiling and the congenital long QT contraindication; escitalopram's label has no QT warning section. Separately, the MHRA does cap escitalopram at 10 mg over age 65 and contraindicates combining it with QT-prolonging drugs, which is where much of the teaching comes from.

sections.title: Good to Know
items: ⚠ Salt and water. Almost every lithium question reduces to this: anything that lowers sodium or body water raises the lithium level.
⚠ Fine tremor = expected. Coarse tremor = toxic. That one word is the difference between reassurance and an emergency.

📌 Davis's and most nursing texts give the therapeutic range as 0.6 to 1.2 mEq/L, and that is the answer on your instructor's exam. The current label is narrower and higher: 0.8 to 1.2 mEq/L titrating for acute mania, and 0.8 to 1.0 mEq/L for maintenance. Both are recorded because a level of 0.7 is therapeutic by one and sub-therapeutic by the other.

items: blocks calcium entry at the neuromuscular junction and depresses CNS excitability → it raises the seizure threshold, which is how it prevents eclamptic seizures

items.action: Monitor URINE OUTPUT hourly and hold for less than 100 mL over 4 hr, which is about 25 mL/hr

items.action: Keep treating the blood pressure separately

sections.title: Good to Know
items: ⚠ The reflexes disappear BEFORE the respirations fall, so absent deep tendon reflexes are your early warning, not the respiratory rate. Sources differ on the numbers: the common nursing triad is RR 12 or more, reflexes present, urine 30 mL/hr or more, while obstetric references use RR above 16 and urine above 25 mL/hr.
⚠ The toxicity order is the whole drug: REFLEXES go, then RESPIRATIONS, then the HEART. Checking the patellar reflex is how you catch it at stage one.

⚠ Magnesium is the anticonvulsant, not the antihypertensive. A preeclamptic patient needs both.

sections.title: Action
items: directly stimulates uterine smooth muscle → a SUSTAINED, forceful contraction rather than the rhythmic pattern oxytocin produces

sections.title: Action
items: binds oxytocin receptors on uterine smooth muscle → rhythmic contractions that ↑ force, frequency and duration
receptor density rises sharply at term → which is why the same dose does little at 20 weeks and a great deal at 40

for postpartum hemorrhage the goal is a CLAMPED uterus, not rhythmic labor → sustained contraction compresses the open spiral arteries at the placental site, and that mechanical compression is what stops the bleeding

items.action: Assess for infection (vital signs, appearance of wound, sputum, urine, stool, WBCs); obtain C&S before the first dose
items.rationale: the drug begins killing immediately, so a culture drawn after the first dose may not grow the organism or reveal its beta-lactamase

items.action: Assess for hypersensitivity and rash (DRESS, SJS, TEN)
items.rationale: these are delayed T-cell mediated hypersensitivity reactions rather than IgE anaphylaxis, so they surface days in and worsen with each further dose

items.action: Check penicillin allergy history
items.rationale: clavulanate does not change the allergy picture, since the beta-lactam ring still carries the IgE risk; documented anaphylaxis or a prior SJS, TEN or DRESS contraindicates it, while a remote nonspecific rash does not

items.action: Assess for diarrhea
items.rationale: clavulanate drives much of the GI upset while the wider spectrum disturbs colonic flora, so diarrhea exceeds plain amoxicillin; food blunts it

items.action: Assess for C. difficile diarrhea
items.rationale: flora loss lets C. difficile overgrow and release toxin → colitis, so this diarrhea is never treated with antidiarrheals, which retain the toxin

items.action: Monitor for S/S of anaphylaxis
items.rationale: beta-lactam sensitization lets IgE drive mast cell degranulation minutes after the dose → laryngeal edema, bronchospasm, and hypotension

items.action: Monitor bowel function
items.rationale: its broader spectrum clears more competing colonic flora than amoxicillin alone, so C. difficile overgrows and releases toxin more readily

items.action: Monitor hepatic panel and assess for jaundice, dark urine, pale stools
items.rationale: clavulanate carries the cholestatic (bile flow is blocked) injury risk, which is idiosyncratic (unpredictable and not dose-related) and can surface after the course ends, so late jaundice and pale stools matter

items.action: Give with food
items.rationale: reduces the diarrhea and GI upset that clavulanate causes
