items.action: Assess for infection (vital signs, appearance of wound, sputum, urine, stool, WBCs); obtain C&S before the first dose
items.rationale: the first dose suppresses bacterial growth and can blank the culture, so C&S precedes it; baseline findings are how you judge response

items.action: Obtain Hx to determine previous penicillin use and any reaction
items.rationale: the beta-lactam ring haptenizes host proteins and drives IgE sensitization, so a prior reaction predicts anaphylaxis on re-exposure

items.action: Assess for hypersensitivity and severe rash (DRESS, SJS, TEN)
items.rationale: these are delayed T-cell mediated reactions to the beta-lactam, and they advance to mucosal erosion and epidermal detachment if dosing continues

items.action: Assess for C. difficile diarrhea
items.rationale: broad anaerobic kill removes the flora that normally suppress C. difficile, so the toxin produces colitis rather than ordinary drug diarrhea

items.action: Monitor for S/S of ANAPHYLAXIS
items.rationale: prior sensitization to the beta-lactam ring lets IgE trigger mast cell degranulation, so histamine release threatens the airway within minutes

items.action: Monitor renal panel (BUN/creatinine)
items.rationale: it is cleared unchanged by the kidney, so a falling GFR accumulates drug, and it can trigger a hypersensitivity acute interstitial nephritis

items.action: Monitor CBC and hepatic panel with prolonged therapy
items.rationale: prolonged exposure can drive immune-mediated neutropenia and a transaminase (AST and ALT) rise, neither of which is symptomatic until the counts or enzymes are checked

items.action: Monitor IV site for phlebitis; rotate infusion sites
items.rationale: the infusion chemically irritates the vein intima, so one site used repeatedly inflames and the line fails before the course is finished

items.action: Monitor bowel function
items.rationale: it kills normal colonic anaerobes along with the pathogen, and losing that flora lets C. difficile overgrow and release toxin

items.action: (PO) Give on an EMPTY stomach, 1 hr before or 2 hr after meals
items.rationale: food reduces absorption

sections.title: Action
items: binds the bacterial 50S ribosomal subunit → blocks protein synthesis. Bacteriostatic, so it stops bacteria multiplying rather than killing them outright
concentrates INSIDE cells and in tissue far above its blood level → which is why it reaches atypical organisms like Chlamydia, Legionella and Mycoplasma that live intracellularly
half-life around 68 hr → the 5-day Z-Pak keeps working for days after the last tablet, and a single 1 g dose treats chlamydia outright

items.action: Assess for a macrolide allergy, and ask specifically about jaundice with a previous course
items.rationale: prior cholestatic (bile flow is blocked) jaundice on azithromycin is a true contraindication, not a caution, and patients do not volunteer it

items.action: Assess for new or worsening diarrhea during and for weeks after therapy
items.rationale: C. difficile can appear up to 2 months after the antibiotic stops. Never treat it with an antidiarrheal

items.action: Obtain cultures BEFORE the first dose
items.rationale: once an antibiotic is in, the culture may not grow the organism, and the therapy cannot be narrowed

items.action: Monitor ECG and K⁺ and Mg²⁺ when other QT drugs are on board
items.rationale: Azithromycin alone rarely causes torsades. Stacked with ondansetron, haloperidol or a low K⁺, it contributes

items.action: Monitor liver function with prolonged or repeated courses
items.rationale: hepatotoxicity ranges from a transaminase (AST and ALT) bump to fulminant failure

items.action: Give with or without food
items.rationale: Both the tablets and the single-dose suspension packet may be taken either way; food raises the tablet peak but leaves total absorption unchanged, and improves tolerability. The old fasting rule belonged to the capsule, a form no longer marketed

items.action: Separate from aluminum- or magnesium-containing antacids by 2 hr
items.rationale: those antacids lower the peak level

items.action: Teach that the course keeps working after the last dose
items.rationale: The 68 hr half-life means a 5-day pack covers about 10 days. Patients think it quit early and ask for more

sections.title: Good to Know
items: ⚠ Macrolide means azithromycin, erythromycin, clarithromycin. All three prolong QT; azithromycin is the gentlest on the stomach and erythromycin the harshest.
⚠ A single 1 g dose for chlamydia is directly observed therapy in the clinic. That is the point: nothing to remember, nothing to stop early.
⚠ The 68 hr half-life is why a 5-day pack covers about 10 days of therapy, and why adherence is better than with erythromycin's four-times-daily dosing.

sections.title: Action
items: inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis → bactericidal, the same mechanism as every other cephalosporin
a SECOND-generation agent → keeps useful gram-positive activity while adding some Haemophilus influenzae and Moraxella reach, which is what ear and sinus infections need

but cefaclor itself is broken down by the beta-lactamases most clinical H. influenzae and Moraxella strains produce → so its coverage of them is less dependable than the class description suggests, and cefuroxime is the second-generation agent actually relied on for H. influenzae
beta-lactamase-negative ampicillin-resistant H. influenzae should be considered resistant to cefaclor even when it looks susceptible in the dish

items.action: Ask what the penicillin reaction actually was
items.rationale: Cross-reactivity is 1 to 2 percent, not 10. Reserve the exclusion for anaphylaxis, angioedema or SJS

items.action: Assess for new diarrhea during and after therapy
items.rationale: broad cell wall killing eliminates the colonic anaerobes that normally outcompete C. difficile, letting spores germinate and release toxins A and B that inflame the mucosa

items.action: Obtain cultures before the first dose
items.rationale: so therapy can be narrowed

items.action: Shake the suspension well and refrigerate it; discard after 14 days
items.rationale: an unshaken suspension delivers an inconsistent dose, and most pediatric dosing errors happen here

items.action: Reduce the dose in renal impairment
items.rationale: cefaclor is excreted largely unchanged by glomerular filtration and tubular secretion, so a low GFR accumulates drug, and beta-lactams at high levels antagonize GABA-A (the brain's main braking receptor) and lower the seizure threshold

items.action: Teach parents to report rash WITH joint pain and fever, especially on a repeat course
items.rationale: That triad is the serum-sickness-like reaction, and cefaclor causes it more than other cephalosporins. It is not a simple drug rash and it means stopping the drug

items: 📌 Source conflict on a number you may be asked. The current Keflex label still says cross-hypersensitivity among beta-lactams may occur in up to 10 percent of penicillin-allergic patients. The allergy literature puts the real figure near 1 percent, and under 1 percent for cephalosporins that do not share an R1 side chain. items.action: Extend the interval to every 48 hours when creatinine clearance is under 30 mL/min, and dose after dialysis

items.action: Do not hold anticoagulation for a prolonged PT/INR without redrawing at TROUGH

sections.title: Action
items: binds the bacterial 30S ribosomal subunit irreversibly → protein synthesis fails and the organism dies. BACTERICIDAL, unlike the bacteriostatic ribosomal agents
killing is CONCENTRATION-dependent → a higher peak kills more, which is why extended-interval dosing gives a large dose once daily rather than small doses often
it needs oxygen-dependent transport to get into the cell → so it does not work on anaerobes at all, and works poorly in an abscess
accumulates in the renal tubule and the inner ear → which is exactly where its two toxicities appear

sections.title: Action
items: inhibits DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV → the bacterium cannot unwind or repackage its own DNA, so replication fails. Bactericidal

a RESPIRATORY fluoroquinolone → it has reliable activity against Streptococcus pneumoniae, which is what makes it a pneumonia drug. Ciprofloxacin has some pneumococcal activity but its own label says it is NOT a drug of first choice for pneumococcal pneumonia
excellent oral bioavailability, close to the IV dose → so IV to PO conversion is one-to-one, which matters for discharge planning

the toxicity has a DIFFERENT mechanism from the antibacterial effect, which is why it is so unpredictable → in tendon it is collagen breakdown driven by matrix metalloproteinase activity plus mitochondrial oxidative stress, and in the CNS it is blockade of inhibitory GABA-A receptors with NMDA stimulation, which is also why it lowers the seizure threshold

hypersensitivity is the only item in the labeled CONTRAINDICATIONS section

the BOXED WARNING separately says to avoid levofloxacin in a known history of myasthenia gravis, because fluoroquinolones may exacerbate muscle weakness → functionally an absolute bar even though it is not filed as a contraindication

items.action: Monitor ECG, K⁺ and Mg²⁺ when other QT drugs are present
items.rationale: fluoroquinolones block the hERG (the potassium channel that resets the heart electrically) potassium channel, and hypokalemia or hypomagnesemia slows repolarization (the heart's electrical reset) further, so each agent's QT effect adds toward torsades de pointes

items.action: Give at least 2 hr BEFORE or 2 hr AFTER calcium, iron, zinc, multivitamins, sucralfate and aluminum or magnesium antacids
items.rationale: Those cations chelate (bind) the drug in the gut and the dose is simply never absorbed, which is a timing failure that looks like treatment failure. Note the window differs by drug: levofloxacin is 2 hr either side, ciprofloxacin is 2 hr before or 6 hr after

items.action: Teach the patient to STOP the drug and call for new tendon, joint or muscle pain, especially in the Achilles
items.rationale: Rupture can follow a single dose and continuing the drug through the pain is what completes the tear. Risk is highest over 60 and with a steroid on board

items.rationale: photosensitivity is marked with the fluoroquinolones

sections.title: Action
items: binds penicillin-binding proteins and blocks cross-linking of the bacterial cell wall → the wall fails and the organism lyses, so it is bactericidal
the carbapenem ring is stable to EXTENDED-SPECTRUM BETA-LACTAMASES, which is what gives it activity where a cephalosporin fails

it is renally excreted, and its 1-beta-methyl group makes it STABLE to renal dehydropeptidase-I → which is why, unlike imipenem, it needs no cilastatin. It is not a meaningful CYP450 substrate, inhibitor or inducer, so its interaction list is short

sections.title: Do Not Give
items: known hypersensitivity to any component or to another carbapenem
demonstrated ANAPHYLACTIC reaction to any beta-lactam
note that a reported penicillin RASH is not a contraindication; only demonstrated anaphylaxis is, and measured carbapenem cross-reactivity in penicillin-allergic patients is under 1 percent
note that a seizure history, renal impairment and concurrent valproate are WARNINGS, not labeled contraindications

groups.label: Serious
items: (Neuro) SEIZURES
(GI) CLOSTRIDIOIDES DIFFICILE ASSOCIATED DIARRHEA
(Derm) SJS
(Derm) TEN
(Derm) DRESS
(Hemat) AGRANULOCYTOSIS
(Misc) ANAPHYLAXIS

groups.label: Common
items: (Neuro) headache
(GI) diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, constipation
(Derm) rash, pruritus
(Hemat) thrombocytopenia, eosinophilia, anemia
(Local) injection site inflammation, phlebitis
(Hepat) ↑ AST and ALT, ↑ bilirubin

items.action: Obtain cultures before the first dose
items.rationale: the drug is bactericidal from the first dose, so an organism that has already been killed may not grow, and the culture is what lets the team narrow therapy off a carbapenem

items.action: Check that the dose and interval match the creatinine clearance
items.rationale: it is renally cleared, and carbapenems antagonise the GABA-A (the brain's main braking receptor), so drug that accumulates in renal impairment is exactly what lowers the seizure threshold

items.action: Check the med list for VALPROATE or divalproex before giving it
items.rationale: carbapenems irreversibly inhibit the enzyme that recycles valproate from its glucuronide (a water-soluble form the kidney can excrete), so the valproate level falls by as much as 80 percent within a day and the patient seizes

items.action: Assess for new diarrhea during therapy and for weeks after
items.rationale: broad killing of colonic anaerobes removes the flora that hold C. difficile down, so its toxin produces colitis rather than ordinary drug diarrhea, and antidiarrheals would retain that toxin

items.action: Monitor the IV site and rotate it
items.rationale: the infusion irritates the vein intima, so one site used for a full course inflames and the access fails before therapy finishes

items.action: Monitor CBC and hepatic panel on prolonged therapy
items.rationale: agranulocytosis, thrombocytopenia and a transaminase (AST and ALT) rise are all silent until the counts or enzymes are checked

items.action: Take a specific allergy history: what happened, and how fast
items.rationale: demonstrated anaphylaxis to any beta-lactam is a labeled contraindication, while a childhood rash is not; measured cross-reactivity is under 1 percent, so a vague allergy label withholds a first-line drug for no benefit

items.action: Give by IV bolus over 3 to 5 min, or infuse over 15 to 30 min
items.rationale: those are the labeled rates, and the reconstituted bolus concentration of 50 mg/mL differs from the diluted infusion concentration

sections.title: Good to Know
items: ⚠ Meropenem does NOT cover MRSA. The label states it outright. It also misses VRE, Stenotrophomonas, the atypicals (Mycoplasma, Chlamydophila, Legionella) and anything carbapenemase-producing.

📌 The FDA indications are only complicated skin infections, complicated intra-abdominal infections, and pediatric meningitis. Sepsis, pneumonia and febrile neutropenia are the usual real reasons it is hanging, and all three are off label.

📌 On paper the labels give meropenem a HIGHER seizure rate (0.7 percent) than imipenem (0.4 percent), which contradicts the standard teaching. Those numbers come from different trials and are not comparable. Controlled meta-analysis against non-carbapenem comparators supports meropenem being the safer one, but head-to-head trials found no difference.
⚠ Meropenem lowers the valproate level, not the reverse. Onset is within a day, recovery takes 1 to 2 weeks after the antibiotic stops, and raising the valproate dose does not rescue it.

sections.title: Action
items: the two drugs block two consecutive steps of bacterial folate synthesis → sequential blockade, which is why the combination is bactericidal when either drug alone is only bacteriostatic
sulfamethoxazole blocks dihydropteroate synthase; trimethoprim blocks dihydrofolate reductase → no folate means no thymidine, no DNA, no replication

humans get folate from the diet rather than making it, which is what makes the drug selective, but the trimethoprim half also inhibits the human enzyme weakly, which is the source of the bone marrow suppression
trimethoprim additionally blocks sodium channels in the distal tubule → less K⁺ excretion → hyperkalemia, which is the interaction that matters most with an ACE inhibitor or ARB
a sulfonamide → the structural reason for the SJS/TEN risk and the cross-reactivity with other sulfa drugs

sections.title: Do Not Give
items: hypersensitivity to sulfonamides or trimethoprim, or Hx of drug-induced immune thrombocytopenia → CROSS-SENSITIVITY with furosemide, thiazides, and celecoxib, all sulfonamide derivatives
marked hepatic damage, and severe renal insufficiency WHEN RENAL FUNCTION CANNOT BE MONITORED → with monitoring it is dosable in renal impairment
megaloblastic anemia secondary to folate deficiency → trimethoprim blocks dihydrofolate reductase and would deepen the deficiency

sections.title: Give With Caution
items: ACE inhibitors, ARBs, or renal impairment → additive hyperkalemia

items.action: Monitor for severe hypersensitivity, anaphylaxis, and severe rash (DRESS, SJS, TEN)

items: inhibits fungal LANOSTEROL 14-ALPHA-DEMETHYLASE (CYP51) → ergosterol is not made, so the fungal cell membrane loses integrity and toxic methylated sterols accumulate
the fungal enzyme is a cytochrome P450, and it is structurally close enough to human CYP2C9 and CYP3A4 that the drug inhibits those too → which is the entire basis of the interaction problem

⚠ For a transplant patient this is the headline interaction on the whole med list: miconazole inhibits intestinal CYP3A4 and roughly DOUBLES the tacrolimus level.

📌 Miconazole is not named in the Prograf label, which lists clotrimazole, fluconazole, itraconazole, ketoconazole, voriconazole and posaconazole. The absence is not safety; the label's general CYP3A inhibitor statement covers it, and the pharmacokinetic data are real.

items.action: Monitor for hyperprolactinemia → menstrual abnormalities, galactorrhea, gynecomastia, sexual dysfunction

items: ⚠ Pick the antiemetic by mechanism: serotonin (chemo, radiation, post-op) → ondansetron. Dopamine + motility (gastroparesis, reflux) → metoclopramide. Dopamine in the CTZ with sedation → prochlorperazine. Vestibular (motion sickness, vertigo) → none of these three; that's an antihistamine or anticholinergic.
⚠ Ondansetron is the antiemetic WITHOUT extrapyramidal reactions as a signature effect: that is its main advantage over the other two in this section.

flashcard.name: Ondansetron
flashcard.indication: Prevention of chemotherapy-induced, radiation-induced, and postoperative nausea and vomiting
flashcard.action: Blocks serotonin at 5-HT3 receptors in vagal nerve terminals in the gut AND in the chemoreceptor trigger zone → the vomiting signal is never sent
nursing_considerations: Contraindicated: congenital long QT syndrome, concurrent apomorphine, PKU (the ODT contains aspartame)
Assess N/V, abdominal distention, and bowel sounds before and after administration
Check K⁺ and Mg²⁺ before IV administration in at-risk patients
Assess for serotonin syndrome → confusion, agitation, dilated pupils, tachycardia, hyperthermia, shivering, hyperreflexia, rigidity, N/V/D, seizures
Assess for extrapyramidal effects → involuntary movements, facial grimacing, rigidity, shuffling gait, hand tremor
Assess for rash
Monitor ECG in Pts. with hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, HF, bradyarrhythmias, or on other QT-prolonging drugs
Give the PONV dose IV over 2 to 5 min; dilute the chemotherapy dose in 50 mL and infuse over 15 min. Never a rapid push, and never more than 16 mg in a single IV dose

quick.one_liner: Phenothiazine → blocks dopamine in the CTZ, plus alpha and muscarinic receptors. Effective, and sedating, and the most side-effect-laden of the three.
watch: BP sitting, standing, and lying → alpha blockade causes orthostatic hypotension
Fall risk → sedation plus orthostasis together
Akathisia and extrapyramidal effects → the most commonly missed adverse effect; giving more drug makes it worse
Tardive dyskinesia → assess q2mo and for 8-12 wk after stopping
CBC → agranulocytosis; a sore throat and fever here means a CBC, not a cold
(IV) Dilute and give slowly; stop for burning or pain
never: Elderly with dementia-related psychosis → ↑ mortality, the black box
quick.working: nausea and vomiting relieved, patient tolerating PO intake

why_this_one.text: Nausea when ondansetron failed, or when sedation is acceptable or even wanted → migraine, vertigo. Most side effects of the three.

(Neuro) TARDIVE DYSKINESIA
(Neuro) NEUROLEPTIC MALIGNANT SYNDROME
(Neuro) SEIZURES

groups.label: Common
items: (EENT) blurred vision, dry eyes
(CV) orthostatic hypotension, tachycardia, ECG changes (Q-wave and T-wave), QT prolongation
(GI) constipation, dry mouth
(Neuro) sedation, akathisia, extrapyramidal reactions

items.action: Assess level of sedation and N/V before and 30-60 min after administration
items.rationale: sedation is the dose-limiting effect; you need the before-and-after to know whether you got antiemesis or just a sleepy patient

items.action: Assess fall risk → drowsiness, orthostatic hypotension, motor and sensory instability
items.rationale: Orthostatic hypotension from alpha-adrenergic blockade plus (Neuro) sedation. Both at once is the highest-risk combination for a fall

items.action: Assess for anticholinergic effects → urinary retention, constipation, dry mouth, blurred vision
items.rationale: anticholinergic activity; older adults are far more sensitive and can become delirious

items.action: Monitor BP sitting, standing, and lying; HR; respiratory rate; and ECG before and frequently during dose adjustment
items.rationale: alpha blockade causes orthostatic hypotension, which only shows up on a positional set of vitals; the drug may also cause Q-wave and T-wave changes and prolong QT

items.action: Monitor for akathisia (restlessness, an inner drive to keep moving) and extrapyramidal effects → parkinsonian (masklike face, shuffling gait, rigidity, tremor) and dystonic (muscle spasms, twisting, twitching)
items.rationale: Extrapyramidal reactions from D2 (the dopamine receptor) blockade. Akathisia is routinely mistaken for anxiety or undertreated nausea, and giving more drug makes it worse

items.action: Monitor for tardive dyskinesia → rhythmic uncontrolled movements of the mouth, face, tongue, and extremities; assess q2mo during therapy and 8-12 wk after discontinuation → report immediately, it may be irreversible
items.rationale: TARDIVE DYSKINESIA; it can emerge after the drug is stopped, which is why the assessment continues past discontinuation

items.action: Monitor for neuroleptic malignant syndrome → fever, severe muscle rigidity, tachycardia, diaphoresis, labile BP, altered consciousness → notify the provider immediately
items.rationale: NMS; mortality is significant and the treatment is stopping the drug plus supportive cooling

items.action: Monitor CBC with differential periodically
items.rationale: AGRANULOCYTOSIS; a sore throat and fever in a patient on a phenothiazine is a CBC, not a cold

items.action: (IV) Dilute and give slowly; stop immediately for burning or pain at the site
items.rationale: Phenothiazines are irritating to vessels and tissue → extravasation causes local injury. This is standard phenothiazine IV practice, not a boxed warning

⚠ Akathisia is the most commonly missed adverse effect here. A patient who 'can't sit still and still feels awful' after a dose is not under-dosed.

quick.one_liner: Phenothiazine → blocks H1 and dopamine receptors centrally, so it treats nausea and allergy and sedates heavily. Directly toxic to tissue parenterally.
watch: NEVER under 2 years of age → fatal respiratory depression

ANY pain or burning at the site → STOP immediately and evaluate for arterial injection

Large patent vein or a central line; never a hand or wrist vein

sections.title: Action
items: blocks H1 histamine receptors centrally, and dopamine receptors in the vomiting center → so it treats nausea and allergy and sedates heavily
it is a PHENOTHIAZINE, so it shares that family's extrapyramidal effects, sedation and anticholinergic burden
it is also profoundly irritating to tissue → the drug itself damages whatever it touches, and that happens by ANY parenteral route, not only when it extravasates
that tissue toxicity is the whole reason for the concentration and rate limits, and it is why deep intramuscular is the preferred parenteral route

intravenous use at concentrations GREATER THAN 1 mg/mL

SUBCUTANEOUS injection → chemical irritation and necrotic lesions
a comatose state

items.action: Assess for extrapyramidal symptoms, akathisia and dystonia; have diphenhydramine or benztropine available
items.rationale: It is a phenothiazine. Restlessness that looks like worsening nausea may be akathisia, and giving more promethazine makes it worse

items.action: Assess BP and pulse before the dose, and again after
items.rationale: It blocks the alpha-1 receptor (the one that tightens blood vessels), so the pressure drops, and the drop is worst after an IV dose and in an older adult

items.action: Monitor respiratory rate and sedation, especially with an opioid on board
items.rationale: it is heavily sedating and additive with every other CNS depressant

items.action: NEVER give it to a child under 2 years of age
items.rationale: A boxed warning and a labeled contraindication. Fatal respiratory depression has occurred. In children over 2 use the lowest effective dose and avoid other respiratory depressants

items.action: Dilute IV doses to no more than 1 mg/mL and give no faster than about 25 mg over 10 min
items.rationale: Exceeding 1 mg/mL is a labeled CONTRAINDICATION, not a caution. The label allows up to 2.5 mL/min for doses up to 50 mg, which at 1 mg/mL is 2.5 mg per minute

items.action: If the patient reports ANY pain or burning at the site during administration, STOP immediately and evaluate for arterial injection or extravasation
items.rationale: This is the one instruction that prevents an amputation. Pain is the first and sometimes only sign, and continuing because the IV still flows is how limbs are lost

items.action: Prefer DEEP INTRAMUSCULAR injection into a large muscle for the parenteral route
items.rationale: The label names deep IM as preferred. Never subcutaneous and never intra-arterial, both labeled contraindications

items.action: Use a large, patent, well-running vein, preferably a central line, and never a hand or wrist vein
items.rationale: small distal veins and areas near arteries are where the catastrophic injuries happen

items.action: Consider whether ondansetron would do the job instead
items.rationale: For routine nausea, a 5-HT3 (the serotonin receptor that triggers vomiting) antagonist carries none of this tissue risk. Raising that is a legitimate nursing contribution

items.action: Know that naloxone does NOT reverse promethazine
items.rationale: The label states this explicitly. There is no reversal agent, which is why prevention is the entire strategy

sections.title: Good to Know
items: 📌 These two boxed warnings belong to PROMETHAZINE, not prochlorperazine. Confusing the two is a common error, and the tissue injury warning in particular is specific to promethazine.
⚠ Maximum IV concentration is 1 mg/mL. Many textbooks and older labels still teach 25 mg/mL; the current label makes exceeding 1 mg/mL a contraindication.
⚠ Pain at the site means stop. Not slow down, not flush, not reassure. Stop.
⚠ No reversal agent exists, and naloxone specifically does not work. Prevention is all there is.

highlight.headline: Makes the bowel move
highlight.critical: BOWEL SOUNDS FIRST → NEVER AGAINST AN OBSTRUCTION

quick.one_liner: Stimulant laxative → irritates the colonic wall and stimulates the myenteric plexus, so peristalsis ↑ and the bowel moves.
watch: Assess bowel sounds and rule out OBSTRUCTION before giving it
Oral dose at BEDTIME → 6 to 12 hr to a morning result
Do not crush or chew; not within 1 hr of an antacid or milk
K⁺ and hydration with repeated use → stimulants waste potassium

never: Give it against a suspected obstruction

quick.working: a soft formed stool within 6 to 12 hr, distension relieved, K⁺ and hydration stable

sections.title: Use
items: short-term relief of constipation
bowel preparation before colonoscopy or surgery
opioid-induced constipation, with a softener

sections.title: Action
items: directly irritates the colonic wall and stimulates the myenteric plexus → peristalsis ↑, so the bowel MOVES. It also reduces water absorption, which softens the stool on the way
it makes the bowel contract rather than softening what is already there → the opposite of docusate, which softens and does not move anything
the oral tablet is enteric-coated to survive the stomach and release in the colon → which is why it must never be crushed or taken with an antacid or milk
oral works in 6 to 12 hr, so it is a bedtime dose for a morning result; the suppository works in 15 to 60 min

sections.title: Do Not Give
items: this is an over-the-counter Drug Facts label with no contraindications section
do not use if the patient cannot swallow the tablet without chewing
ask a provider first with a sudden change in bowel habits lasting more than 2 weeks, or with stomach pain, nausea or vomiting → those are the signals of an obstruction

sections.title: Give With Caution
items: a suspected bowel OBSTRUCTION is the clinical absolute: stimulating peristalsis against a blockage risks perforation

groups.label: Serious
items: (F&E) HYPOKALEMIA and dehydration with chronic use

groups.label: Common
items: (GI) abdominal cramping and griping, nausea, diarrhea, rectal burning with the suppository
(F&E) electrolyte loss
(GI) laxative dependence and a hypotonic colon with long-term use
(Misc) protein-losing enteropathy with chronic abuse

items.action: Assess bowel sounds and rule out obstruction before giving it
items.rationale: Stimulating peristalsis against a mechanical obstruction can perforate the bowel. Absent bowel sounds with distension and vomiting means hold the drug and call

items.action: Assess and document the result: time, amount and consistency
items.rationale: the therapeutic endpoint, and the only way to know whether to repeat it

items.action: Monitor K⁺ and hydration with repeated use
items.rationale: stimulant laxatives waste potassium, which matters most in a patient on digoxin or a diuretic

items.action: Give the oral dose at BEDTIME and explain the 6 to 12 hr timing
items.rationale: A morning result. Patients who take it in the morning spend the day cramping and conclude it did not work

items.action: Do not crush or chew the tablet, and do not give it within 1 hr of an antacid or milk
items.rationale: The enteric coating releases the drug in the colon. Breaking it causes gastric irritation and loses the effect

items.action: For opioid-induced constipation, expect a softener plus a stimulant
items.rationale: Opioids slow the gut and harden the stool, so you need both jobs done. A softener alone is the classic undertreatment

items.action: Position on the left side for the suppository and have the patient retain it 15 to 20 min
items.rationale: anatomy of the sigmoid, and retention time is what lets it work

items.action: Teach that this is SHORT-term and address the actual cause
items.rationale: Chronic stimulant use produces a dependent, hypotonic colon. Fiber, fluids and mobility are the durable answer

items: diphenoxylate is an opioid that slows intestinal motility → the same mechanism as loperamide, so contents stay longer and water is reabsorbed

sections.title: Action
items: an opioid agonist on the mu receptors of the GUT wall → slows peristalsis, so contents stay in the bowel longer and more water is reabsorbed. Fewer, firmer stools
at normal doses it barely crosses the blood-brain barrier → so it has the constipating effect of an opioid without euphoria or analgesia, which is why it is sold over the counter

at HIGH doses two separate things go wrong. Saturating the pump that keeps it out of the brain lets it act centrally → euphoria and respiratory depression, which is why it is abused. And high plasma levels block cardiac potassium and SODIUM channels directly, which the heart was never protected from → QT prolongation, a widened QRS, torsades and cardiac arrest. That cardiac effect is the basis of the boxed warning
slowing the bowel is exactly the wrong move in a toxin-mediated infection → it traps the toxin against the mucosa instead of expelling it

items.action: Assess hydration and electrolytes, and treat those first
items.rationale: the fluid and potassium loss is what actually harms the patient; stopping the stool is symptom control

items.action: Ask about substance use and screen for misuse
items.rationale: Loperamide is used deliberately as an opioid substitute at enormous doses. An early refill or a patient buying it in bulk is the signal

items.action: Check for other QT-prolonging drugs

items.action: HOLD it and call for diarrhea with blood, fever, or recent antibiotic exposure
items.rationale: In an invasive or toxin-mediated infection, slowing the bowel traps the pathogen and its toxin. C. difficile colitis treated with loperamide becomes toxic megacolon. This is the single most important judgment with the drug

items.action: Never give it to a child under 2, and get advice for ages 2 to 5
items.rationale: labeled contraindication under 2, and respiratory and CNS depression in small children

items.action: Teach the DOSE CEILING explicitly and warn about cardiac death from exceeding it
items.rationale: OTC maximum is 8 mg in 24 hr, prescription maximum 16 mg. The boxed warning exists because people take dozens of tablets, and patients genuinely do not know it can stop their heart

items.action: Teach that it controls the symptom and does not treat the cause
items.rationale: diarrhea beyond 48 hr, or with fever or blood, needs a diagnosis

sections.title: Action
items: binds dietary phosphate in the gut to form an insoluble calcium phosphate complex → excreted in the feces instead of absorbed → ↓ serum phosphorus
it works in the gut lumen, not in the blood → which is why it only works if it is in the stomach at the same time as the food

failing kidneys can't excrete phosphate → phosphate rises → it binds circulating calcium → calcium falls → PTH rises → bone is resorbed to supply calcium (renal osteodystrophy), and calcium-phosphate product deposits in vessels and soft tissue

sections.title: Do Not Give
items: hypercalcemia → the binder is a calcium load

sections.title: Give With Caution
items: AVOID other calcium supplements, including over-the-counter calcium-based antacids → additive calcium load
separate TETRACYCLINES and FLUOROQUINOLONES → give them at least 1 hr before the binder, whose calcium chelates them
separate LEVOTHYROXINE by at least 4 hr before or 4 hr after → absorption falls otherwise
review vitamin D → the label recommends reducing or stopping it, because it raises calcium absorption on top of the binder

items.action: Assess bowel function and treat constipation

items.action: Assess for hypercalcemia → lethargy, confusion, N/V, constipation, bone pain, polyuria
items.rationale: the binder is itself a calcium salt and a fraction is absorbed, so the load raises serum calcium, especially when vitamin D analogs are increasing gut uptake

items.action: Monitor serum calcium twice weekly during dose titration → hold or discontinue if Ca²⁺ >12 mg/dL
items.rationale: hypercalcemia; the calcium you give to bind phosphate is partly absorbed

items.action: Monitor serum phosphorus
items.rationale: the therapeutic target; phosphorus should fall toward normal, and a normal phosphorus with a high calcium means the dose is too high or needs a non-calcium binder

items.action: Monitor Pts. on digoxin for signs of toxicity → anorexia, N/V, visual changes, bradycardia, arrhythmias
items.rationale: Hypercalcemia potentiates (strengthens) digoxin at the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase → digoxin toxicity at a therapeutic level. This is the interaction the card exists to warn you about

items.action: Give WITH meals
items.rationale: the drug binds phosphate in food; given between meals there is no phosphate to bind and all you've delivered is a calcium load

sections.title: Action
items: binds to bone and is taken up by OSTEOCLASTS, the cells that break bone down → the osteoclast cannot function and dies, so resorption slows while formation continues
it does not build new bone directly; it stops the loss → so density rises slowly over months and the real endpoint is a fracture that does not happen
absorption is terrible, under one percent, and ANY food, drink or other medication destroys it → which is why the administration rules are so rigid and are most of the drug
it has a half-life in bone measured in YEARS → so the effect persists long after the drug is stopped, which is the basis of the drug holiday

hypersensitivity to any component, including urticaria and angioedema
do not give the oral solution to patients at ↑ risk of aspiration

sections.title: Action
items: the striatum balances dopamine against acetylcholine → when dopamine falls, or an antipsychotic blocks it, acetylcholine is left unopposed and the result is tremor, rigidity and dystonia
benztropine blocks the muscarinic acetylcholine receptor → it restores the balance by lowering the cholinergic side rather than raising dopamine
that is why it works within MINUTES on an acute dystonic reaction → it is treating a neurotransmitter imbalance directly, and the relief is dramatic and immediate
it is better for TREMOR than for bradykinesia → so in Parkinson disease it is an adjunct, not a substitute for levodopa

sections.title: Do Not Give
items: hypersensitivity to benztropine or any component
children UNDER 3 YEARS of age, because of its atropine-like effects → a genuine labeled contraindication, with caution in older children

angle-closure glaucoma is NOT a labeled contraindication; the label says in Precautions that it probably should not be used in angle-closure glaucoma, and that it does not appear to affect simple glaucoma

items.action: Do NOT give it for TARDIVE DYSKINESIA; it can make it worse

items.rationale: Blocked sweating means the body cannot cool. Hyperthermia on an anticholinergic is a medical emergency

sections.title: Action
items: Parkinson disease is a dopamine deficiency, but dopamine itself cannot cross the blood-brain barrier → LEVODOPA can, and once inside the brain it is converted to dopamine
the problem is that most levodopa is converted to dopamine in the PERIPHERY before it ever reaches the brain, which causes nausea and hypotension and wastes the dose

CARBIDOPA blocks that peripheral conversion and does NOT cross into the brain → so more levodopa reaches the CNS, the dose can be about 75 percent lower, and the nausea is far less. Carbidopa has no antiparkinson effect of its own
after years of therapy the response narrows into ON and OFF periods with dyskinesias → which is disease progression showing through the drug rather than drug failure

sections.title: Do Not Give

known hypersensitivity to any component
NARROW-ANGLE GLAUCOMA → this is a genuine labeled contraindication
melanoma is NOT a contraindication; the label notes in Precautions that Parkinson patients have a 2 to 6 fold higher melanoma risk, so skin surveillance is advised

items.action: Assess for dyskinesia versus rigidity and record WHEN in the dosing cycle it happens
items.rationale: Dyskinesia is too much and rigidity is too little. The timing is what lets the dose be adjusted, and nursing observation is the only source of it

items.action: Ask specifically about hallucinations, new gambling, shopping or sexual behavior
items.rationale: Impulse control disorders are a recognized dopaminergic effect, families are ashamed to raise them, and they resolve when the dose is adjusted. You have to ask

items.action: Give doses ON TIME, to the minute, and do not let them be held for routine reasons
items.rationale: This is the central nursing issue in Parkinson care. A dose an hour late can leave a patient rigid, unable to swallow or walk, and at risk of aspiration and falls. Hospital routines are the usual cause, and advocating for exact timing is real nursing work

items.action: Separate it from HIGH-PROTEIN meals
items.rationale: Levodopa is an amino acid and competes with dietary amino acids for the same transporter into the brain. A protein-heavy meal can abolish the dose. Spread protein to later in the day

items.action: Never stop it abruptly

sections.title: Action
items: a manufactured version of erythropoietin, the hormone the KIDNEY makes to tell the bone marrow to produce red cells → in kidney failure the kidney stops making it, which is the cause of the anemia
it replaces the signal, so the marrow makes red cells again → but it needs raw material, which is why IRON must be adequate or the drug simply does not work

sections.title: Action
items: supplies the iron the body needs to build HEMOGLOBIN → it does not stimulate the marrow, it supplies the raw material, so it only helps when iron is the thing that is missing
it is absorbed in the duodenum in the FERROUS (Fe2+) form, and absorption improves in an acid environment → which is why vitamin C helps and why antacids and PPIs hurt
only about 20 percent of ferrous sulfate by weight is elemental IRON → so a 325 mg tablet provides about 65 mg of actual iron, and that is the number that matters

the response is slow and sequential → reticulocytes rise in about a week, hemoglobin over weeks, and the iron STORES take 3 to 6 months to refill, which is why therapy continues long after the blood count is normal

sections.title: Do Not Give
items: this is an over-the-counter label with no contraindications section
clinically avoid it in hemochromatosis and other iron overload states, and in hemolytic anemia where iron is not the problem

the pediatric iron poisoning statement is presented as a BOXED WARNING on some labels and as an OTC warning on others, because iron reaches the market as an unapproved drug, an OTC monograph product and a supplement → check the product in hand

sections.title: Action
items: a sugar alcohol that is FILTERED by the glomerulus and then not reabsorbed → it stays in the tubule, holds water osmotically, and that water leaves as urine

it also pulls fluid OUT of the brain and the eye into the vascular space, because it does not cross an intact blood-brain barrier → the osmotic gradient is what reduces intracranial and intraocular pressure

that same mechanism means it transiently EXPANDS the intravascular volume before the diuresis → which is why it can precipitate pulmonary edema and heart failure in a patient whose heart cannot handle the load
it crystallizes at low temperature → so the solution is inspected, warmed if needed, and given through a filter

sections.title: Do Not Give
items: known hypersensitivity to mannitol
ANURIA → if the kidney is not filtering, the drug cannot work and simply accumulates
SEVERE HYPOVOLEMIA
pre-existing severe pulmonary vascular congestion or PULMONARY EDEMA
ACTIVE INTRACRANIAL BLEEDING, except during craniotomy → note that carve-out
oliguria is NOT a contraindication; anuria is

groups.label: Serious

(F&E) DEHYDRATION
(F&E) HYPOKALEMIA
(GU) ACUTE KIDNEY INJURY, especially at high cumulative doses
(Neuro) REBOUND INTRACRANIAL PRESSURE after prolonged use
(Local) TISSUE NECROSIS with extravasation

groups.label: Common
items: (CV) hypotension after the diuresis, hypertension, tachycardia
(F&E) hypernatremia or hyponatremia, metabolic acidosis, osmotic gap
(GU) osmotic nephrosis, urinary retention

(Local) thrombophlebitis

items.action: VITALS BEFORE AND AFTER: BP, AND URINE OUTPUT, BEFORE THE DOSE AND HOURLY AFTER
items.rationale: Hold and call if urine output does not rise, which means the dose is staying in the circulation → (CV) the sequence is expansion, then brisk diuresis, then a volume deficit. Each phase needs different management

items.action: Inspect for CRYSTALS; if present, warm the container with agitation, then ALLOW IT TO COOL to room or body temperature and re-inspect before use. Always give it through an administration set with a FILTER
items.rationale: Mannitol crystallizes when cold and infusing crystals is dangerous, but the cooling step is not optional: Osmitrol is warmed to about 70 degrees C and the 25 percent vial to about 80 degrees C, and infusing fluid at that temperature would cause thermal injury and hemolysis. Warm it, cool it, look again, filter it. Do not use a microwave or a water bath

items.action: Assess lung sounds, jugular venous distension and oxygen saturation
items.rationale: The transient volume expansion that precedes the diuresis is what causes pulmonary edema in a failing heart. This is the deterioration that happens in the first minutes

items.action: Assess the IV site frequently and use a large vein
items.rationale: It is hyperosmolar and extravasation causes tissue necrosis. The 25 percent solution is about 1372 mOsmol/L

items.action: Confirm the patient is not anuric before giving it
items.rationale: anuria is a labeled contraindication, and it is the distinction from oliguria that gets tested

items.action: Monitor serum and urine OSMOLALITY, sodium, potassium and renal function frequently
items.rationale: therapy is guided by osmolality rather than by the dose, and the drug both dehydrates and shifts electrolytes

items.action: Monitor neurologic status and intracranial pressure continuously if monitored
items.rationale: The therapeutic endpoint. Also watch for REBOUND intracranial pressure after prolonged therapy, when mannitol has leaked into brain tissue and starts pulling water the other way

items.action: Insert a urinary catheter and monitor output HOURLY
items.rationale: the diuresis is brisk, and the drug is held if the patient stops producing urine, because mannitol that is not excreted accumulates and expands the intravascular space with nowhere to go

items.action: Never give it with blood through the same line
items.rationale: it causes agglutination and crenation of red cells

items: releases bicarbonate ions → buffers excess hydrogen ion → ↑ serum pH, correcting metabolic acidosis

items.action: Assess for hypokalemia → weakness, fatigue, U wave on ECG, arrhythmias, polyuria, polydipsia

sections.title: Action
items: suppresses hepatic synthesis and secretion of cholesterol and inhibits its intestinal absorption → bile becomes cholesterol-solubilizing rather than cholesterol-precipitating, so an existing cholesterol stone dissolves slowly from the surface inward
as a HYDROPHILIC bile acid it displaces toxic hydrophobic bile acids from the bile acid pool → which is the separate mechanism behind its use in cholestatic liver disease
it is cytoprotective to bile duct epithelium and stimulates bile flow → so it lowers alkaline phosphatase and GGT without curing the underlying disease
about 90 percent of an oral dose is absorbed in the small bowel and then heavily extracted by the liver on first pass, and it recirculates enterohepatically, so steady state takes roughly 3 weeks

sections.title: Do Not Give
items: calcified cholesterol stones, radiopaque stones and radiolucent bile pigment stones, which it will not dissolve
acute cholecystitis, cholangitis, biliary obstruction, gallstone pancreatitis and biliary-gastrointestinal fistula
allergy to bile acids
(Urso) complete biliary obstruction
note that elevated liver enzymes and pregnancy are precautions rather than labeled contraindications

groups.label: Common
items: (GI) diarrhea, abdominal pain, nausea, dyspepsia, +2 more
(MS) back pain, arthralgia, myalgia
(Neuro) headache, dizziness, fatigue
(Derm) rash, pruritus, alopecia
(Hepat) worsening of pre-existing liver disease

items.action: Expect ultrasound every 6 months during the first year
items.rationale: the label uses imaging rather than symptoms to judge response, and no partial dissolution by 12 months predicts that continuing is unlikely to help

items.action: Review for estrogens, oral contraceptives and clofibrate
items.rationale: all three ↑ hepatic cholesterol secretion, which works directly against the drug's whole mechanism

items.action: Monitor liver enzymes and bilirubin monthly for 3 months, then every 6 months in PBC
items.rationale: that is the labeled schedule, and a significant rise from a stable baseline is the signal to consider stopping rather than a routine fluctuation

items.action: Monitor a transplant patient's calcineurin inhibitor trough after starting or stopping it
items.rationale: improving bile flow can change how much of a bile-dependent drug is solubilized and absorbed, and the evidence is strongest for cyclosporine

items.action: Give the PBC dose in divided doses WITH food
items.rationale: dividing the dose keeps the bile continuously desaturated rather than letting it resaturate between doses, and the Urso label specifies food

items.action: Separate it from cholestyramine, colestipol and ALUMINUM-containing antacids
items.rationale: those agents adsorb bile acids in the gut and reduce the amount of ursodiol absorbed, so giving them together simply removes the drug

items.action: ⚠ Only radiolucent, NONCALCIFIED cholesterol stones under 20 mm dissolve
items.rationale: the drug works by desaturating bile of cholesterol, so a stone made of pigment or wrapped in calcium has nothing for it to dissolve away

items.action: Teach that dissolution takes months and up to 2 years, with no symptom to track
items.rationale: stones dissolve from the surface inward at a rate set by bile composition, so a patient who expects a quick result stops the drug long before it could have worked

items.action: Report new obstructive symptoms: worsening right upper quadrant pain, vomiting or jaundice
items.rationale: a stone that moves during dissolution can obstruct the duct, and the label asks for the drug to be held while that is evaluated

sections.title: Good to Know
items: ⚠ It only dissolves radiolucent, NONCALCIFIED CHOLESTEROL stones under 20 mm. It does nothing for pigment, calcified or radiopaque stones. About 30 percent of unselected patients achieve complete dissolution over up to 2 years, rising to about 81 percent when the stones are 5 mm or smaller.

📌 Actigall and Urso are different products. Actigall is for gallstones at 8 to 10 mg/kg/day; Urso 250 and Urso Forte are for primary biliary cholangitis at 13 to 15 mg/kg/day with food. One monograph cannot be right for both.
📌 The separation interval from antacids and sequestrants is practice convention. The ursodiol label states the interaction but gives no number.
⚠ Ursodiol is a bile ACID, not a bile acid SEQUESTRANT. It does not bind levothyroxine, and the levothyroxine separation rule that gets extrapolated onto it has no basis.
